human_translations.translator_1: A thousand lords with girdle-jade walk in front and rear. The many flags of guardsmen stand both left and right. Those holding gilt bludgeons, And halberds and axes, March in pairs and pairs; The red silk lanterns, The royal incense urn, Move in solemnity. The dragons fly and the phoenixes dance; The falcons soar and the eagles take wing. This Son of Heaven’s an upright sage; The righteous ministers are good. They increase our bliss by a thousand years, surpassing Yu and Shun; They secure peace of ten thousand ages, rivaling Yao and Tang. We also see the curve-handled umbrella, And robes with rolling dragons— Their glare lighting up each other; The jade joined-rings, The phoenix fans, Waving through holy mist. Those caps of pearls and belts of jade; The purple sashes and medals of gold. A thousand rows of soldiers protect the Throne; Two lines of marshals uphold the carriage. This emperor, cleansed and sincere, bows to the Buddha, Glad to raise incense and seek virtue’s fruit. The grand cortege of the Tang emperor soon arrived in front of the temple. The emperor ordered a halt to the music, left the carriages, and led many officials in the worship of Buddha by taking up burning incense sticks in their hands. After bowing three times holding the incense, they raised their heads and looked around them. This was indeed a splendid religious hall. You see Dancing flags and banners; Bright, gleaming sunshades. Dancing flags and banners Fill the air with strands of flashing colored mists. Bright, gleaming sunshades Glow in the sun as fiery bolts. Imposing, the gold image of Lokājyeṣṭha;14 Most awesome, the jade features of the arhats. Divine flowers fill the vases. Sandalwood incense burn in the urns. The divine flowers filling the vases Adorn the temple with a brilliant forest of brocade. The sandalwood incense burning in the urns Covers the clear sky with waves of fragrant clouds. Piled high on red trays are fruits in season. On colored counters, mounds of cakes and sweets rest. Rows of noble priests chant the holy sūtras To save from their travails those orphaned souls. Taizong and his officials each lifted the incense; they also worshipped the golden body of the Buddha and paid homage to the arhats. Thereafter, the Master of the Law, Chen Xuanzang, the Grand Expositor of the Faith, led the various monks to greet the Tang emperor. After the ceremony, they went back to their seats according to their rank and station. The priest then presented Taizong with the proclamation for the deliverance of the orphaned souls. It read: The supreme virtue is vast and endless, for Buddhism is founded upon Nirvāṇa. The spirit of the pure and the clean circulates freely and flows everywhere in the Three Regions. There are a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations, all regulated by the forces of yin and yang. Boundless and vast indeed are the substance, the function, the true nature, and the permanence of such phenomena. But look at those orphaned souls, how worthy they are of our pity and commiseration! Now by the holy command of Taizong, we have selected and assembled various priests, who will engage in meditation and in the proclamation of the Law. Flinging wide the gates of salvation and setting in motion many vessels of mercy, we would deliver you, the multitudes, from the Sea of Woe and save you from perdition and from the Sixfold Path. You will be led to return to the way of truth and to enjoy the bliss of Heaven. Whether it be by motion, rest, or nonactivity, you will be united with, and become, pure essences. Therefore make use of this noble occasion, for you are invited to the pleasures of the celestial city. Take advantage of our Grand Mass so that you may find release from Hell’s confinement, ascend quickly and freely to ultimate bliss, and travel without restraint in the Region of the West.15 The poem says: An urn of immortal incense. Some scrolls of salvific power. As we proclaim this boundless Law, Receive now Heaven’s endless grace. All your guilt and crime abolished, You lost souls may leave your prison. May our nation be firmly blessed With peace long and all-embracing. Highly pleased by what he read, Taizong said to the monks, “Be firm, all of you, in your devotion, and do not slack in your service to Buddha. After the achievement of merit and after each has received his blessing, we shall reward you handsomely. Be assured that you will not have labored in vain.”
human_translations.translator_2: There was no thunder and no lightning after this. This made the Wizard still more anxious, and he burnt more incense and charms and recited more incantations and struck the table as his fourth signal. Instantly the dragons from the four oceans appeared. Sun cried out above their heads, “Aoguang, where do you think you are going?” Aoguang and his companions came forward and bowed. Then Sun told them what he had told the other helpers before, and added, “You helped me before though not successfully. Today I hope you will help me with success.” The Dragon King replied, “I gladly obey your orders.” Sun said, “I beg of you to give me a helping hand. The Wizard’s signal of the fourth performance is now finished. It is now my turn, and I expect you all to help me. I burn no incense and have no signal but my club. When I lift up my spear the first time, I want the wind to blow.” The Mistress of the Wind said, “The wind shall blow.” “When I lift up my spear the second time, I want the clouds to gather.” The Master of the Clouds said, “The clouds shall gather.” “When I lift up my spear the third time, I want thunder and lightning.” The Master of Thunder and Mistress of Lightning said, “You shall have them in abundance.” “When I lift up my spear the fourth time, I want rain.” The Dragon replied, “Your orders shall be obeyed.” “When I lift up my spear the fifth time, I want a clear sky without fail.” Having arranged this, he restored the false Sun and took his place. He shouted out, “Master Wizard, your fourth signal for performance is now over and there has been neither wind, clouds, thunder, lightning, nor rain. Now it is my time to try.” The Wizard came down from his platform altar and went to the gallery by the king, and the Monkey followed him. The king asked the wizard how it was that none of his four attempts were successful. The wizard replied, “The rain king was not at home today.” The Monkey angrily replied, “The dragon gods were all at home, but your Royal Wizard is not sufficiently skilful.” The king then ordered the Buddhist monks to mount the platform. Sun invited the Master to go, but he said he could not command rain.
human_translations.translator_3: “How wonderful!” gasped all present—including the emperor—kneeling, bowing, and burning incense. Taizong called quickly for a skilled painter to sketch a true likeness of the Bodhisattva, but as soon as the artist lifted his brush, the vision vaporized, leaving only a slip of paper drifting down on the breeze. On it was written the following message: Greetings, Emperor of the Tang! 108,000 miles west of here, wonderful texts speak of the Mahayana. Once distributed throughout your empire, these sutras will deliver the ghosts of the damned from Hell. He who is willing to seek them will become a golden Buddha. “Let’s pause the mass and our pursuit of virtue until someone has brought back these miraculous scriptures,” decided the emperor. “But who will go?” asked his officials. “Though entirely useless,” Xuanzang instantly spoke up, “I volunteer to fetch these treasures that will secure the empire in perpetuity.” The emperor immediately raised Xuanzang to his feet and bowed four times to him. “For such sacrifice and service, we will become brothers.” “I swear on my life to reach the Western Heaven,” Xuanzang responded, overwhelmed. “If not, I will never return home and instead pass straight to Hell.” The beaming emperor now returned to the palace, to prepare Xuanzang’s travel documents and await an auspicious day for his departure. Xuanzang, meanwhile, went back to his own temple, which was buzzing with the news of his pledge. “Did you really volunteer to go to the Western Heaven?” one of his disciples asked him. “The way is full of tigers, leopards, demons, and monsters, wide rivers and high mountains. Will we ever see you again?” “I have made a solemn oath,” said Xuanzang. “I must repay the emperor’s generosity by serving the country. If I fail, I will be damned to eternal perdition. Remember: The active mind conjures up demons; the stilled mind extinguishes them. I may be gone for two, three, seven years, or forever. But if the pine tree inside our gate points eastward, you’ll know that I’ll be back soon.” The next morning at court, Taizong wrote out a document describing the mission and stamped it with an imperial seal granting free passage to its bearer. “The stars are auspiciously aligned today for the start of a long journey,” the Department of Astronomy reported.
human_translations.translator_4: A thousand officials with jade at their belts walked in due order. The banners of the five guards are drawn up on either side. Holding golden gourds, Wielding battle-axes, They stand in pairs; Lamps of purple gauze, Imperial censers, Make majestic clouds. Dragons fly and phoenixes dance, Ospreys and eagles soar. True is the enlightened Son of Heaven, Good are his just and loyal ministers. This age of prosperity surpasses the time of Shun and Yu; The eternal peace he has given outdoes that of Yao and Tang. Under a parasol with curved handle The dragon robe sweeps in, Dazzling bright. Interlocking jade rings, Coloured phoenix fans, Shimmer with a magic glow. Pearl crowns and belts of jade, Gold seals on purple cords. A thousand regiments of soldiers protect the imperial chariot, Two lines of generals carry the royal chair. Bathed and reverent, the Emperor comes to worship the Buddha, Submitting to the True Achievement as he joyfully burns incense. When the carriage of the Tang Emperor reached the temple, orders were given to stop the music as he descended from the vehicle and went at the head of his officials to bow to the Buddha and burn incense. When he had done this three times he looked up and saw what a magnificent assembly it was: Dancing banners, Flying canopies. When the banners danced The sky shook with the clouds of silk; When the canopies flew The sun gleamed as the red lightning flashed. Perfect the image of the statue of the Honoured One, Mighty the grandeur of the Arhats' countenances. Magic flowers in a vase, Censers burning sandalwood and laka. As the fairy flowers stand in vases Trees like brocade fill the temple with their brightness. As the censers burn sandalwood and laka Clouds of incense rise to the azure heaven. Fresh fruit of the season is piled in vermilion dishes, Exotic sweets are heaped on the silk-covered tables. Serried ranks of holy monks intone the surras To save abandoned souls from suffering. Taizong and his civil and military officials all burned incense, bowed to the golden body of the Lord Buddha, and paid their respects to the Arhats. The Hierarch Chen Xuanzang then led all the monks to bow to the Emperor, and when this was over they divided into their groups and went to their meditation places while the Hierarch showed the Emperor the notice about the delivery of the lonely ghosts. It read: “Mysterious is the ultimate virtue, and the Sect of Meditation leads to Nirvana. The purity of the truth is all-knowing; it pervades the Three Regions of the universe. Through its countless changes it controls the Negative and Positive; unbounded are the embodiments of the eternal reality. In considering those forlorn ghosts one should be deeply distressed. At the sacred command of Taizong we have assembled some chosen monks for meditation and preaching. He has opened wide the gates of enlightenment and rowed far the boat of mercy, saving all the beings in the sea of suffering, and delivering those who had long been afflicted by the six ways of existence. They will be led back to the right road and revel in the great chaos; in action and in passivity they will be at one with primal simplicity. For this wonderful cause they are invited to see the purple gates of the pure capital, and through our assembly they will escape from the confines of Hell to climb to the World of Bliss and be free, wandering as they please in the Paradise of the West. As the poem goes: A burner of incense of longevity, A few spells to achieve rebirth. The infinite Law is proclaimed, The boundless mercy of Heaven is shown. When sins are all washed away, The neglected souls leave Hell. We pray to protect our country; May it stay at peace and be blessed.” When he had read this the Tang Emperor's heart was filled with happiness and he said to the monks, “Hold firm to your sincerity and never allow yourselves a moment's slackness in the service of the Buddha. Later on, when the Assembly is over, you will be blessed and we shall richly reward you. You shall certainly not have labored in vain.” The twelve hundred monks all kowtowed to thank him.

translation:
Thousand officials surrounded the Emperor, their emblems fanning out before and behind. The guards stood in rows on either side, swords and axes gleaming, in pairs facing each other.  Red silk candles flickered, while incense burned in ornate censers, filling the hall with a rich, palpable fragrance. Dragons soared and phoenixes took flight, as eagles and falcons spread their wings. The divinely appointed Son of Heaven, the Emperor, sat upright, surrounded by loyal and righteous ministers. His virtues have surpassed those of Shun and Yu from a thousand years past, his rule will rival that of Yao and Tang, bringing prosperity for ten thousand generations.

A sight to behold! The Emperor's scepter and throne are covered in brocade, their brilliance intermingling. Jade bracelets and intricately painted fans adorned with phoenixes cast down a scattering of auspicious light.  He wears a crown of jewels and a sash of purple, adorned with golden emblems. Thousands of soldiers stand guard, escorting the Emperor in two long lines. This Emperor, in utmost sincerity and reverence, bathes in the presence of the Buddha, taking refuge in the teachings and offering fragrant incense. 

Before the temple, the Tang King arrived early, silencing the music and instruments. He stepped out of his carriage, accompanied by many officials, prostrated himself before the Buddha, and offered incense. After three circuits, he looked up and saw indeed a magnificent assembly hall. Flags and banners fluttered, their colors brilliant.  The banners danced in the air, the swirling rainbow clouds seemed to shimmer. The jeweled canopy shone, its reflections illuminating the vibrant, crimson streaks of sunlight.

The Buddha, with his golden elephant-like form, emanates an aura of serenity. The Bodhisattvas, adorned with jade, radiate an aura of unwavering strength.  The incense burner offered an array of beautiful flowers, while sandalwood burned, releasing its sweet fragrance.  The fragrant sandalwood rose high, filling the air with a gentle mist. On a red lacquer tray were arranged exquisite fruits, and on a colorful altar, unique candies and pastries were stacked high. High priests and monks chanted the sacred sutras, praying to liberate lost souls from their suffering.

Emperor Taizong, both civil and military officials, offered incense, bowed before the golden Buddha, and respectfully paid homage to the Bodhisattvas. He saw Master Xuanzang, the renowned Buddhist master, leading the assembled monks in a respectful bow towards the Tang King. The ceremony completed, the monks took their designated meditation spots, and the Master presented the Emperor with a scroll titled, "A Charter for Liberating Souls," which read:

"Great virtue transcends understanding, Zen embodies emptiness. Pure and insightful, it flows through the three realms. Its forms are ever-changing, encompassing both yin and yang. Its essence is true and eternal, boundless and limitless. Observing those lost souls, one should feel deep compassion. Following the Emperor's holy command, we have gathered these monks to practice Zen and preach the Dharma. We open the door to convenience, spreading our compassionate vessel,  to ferry all living beings across the ocean of suffering, freeing them from the ailments of the six realms. Guide them to the true path, immerse them in the primordial chaos; let stillness and action be without striving, blending into pure simplicity. Relying on this auspicious occasion, we invite blessings upon the peaceful capital; utilize this fortunate gathering, free yourselves from the confines of hell and the mortal world.  Ascend to the Pure Land, enjoy boundless freedom, and come and go freely to the West.

As the poem states:
One incense burner burns eternally, 
A few scrolls lead to rebirth. 
Infinite wondrous Dharma is proclaimed, 
Eternal blessings rain down. 
All grievances are extinguished, 
All lost souls are released. 
May this protect my nation, 
Bringing peace and prosperity for ten thousand years. "

The Emperor, reading this, felt immense joy. He addressed the monks: “You have virtuous hearts, do not neglect your Buddhist duties. After this task is complete, and you have all achieved your rewards, I will reward you generously, never letting your efforts go unrewarded."  The twelve hundred monks bowed in unison, expressing their gratitude.

human_translations.translator_3: “How wonderful!” gasped all present—including the emperor—kneeling, bowing, and burning incense. Taizong called quickly for a skilled painter to sketch a true likeness of the Bodhisattva, but as soon as the artist lifted his brush, the vision vaporized, leaving only a slip of paper drifting down on the breeze. On it was written the following message: Greetings, Emperor of the Tang! 108,000 miles west of here, wonderful texts speak of the Mahayana. Once distributed throughout your empire, these sutras will deliver the ghosts of the damned from Hell. He who is willing to seek them will become a golden Buddha. “Let’s pause the mass and our pursuit of virtue until someone has brought back these miraculous scriptures,” decided the emperor. “But who will go?” asked his officials. “Though entirely useless,” Xuanzang instantly spoke up, “I volunteer to fetch these treasures that will secure the empire in perpetuity.” The emperor immediately raised Xuanzang to his feet and bowed four times to him. “For such sacrifice and service, we will become brothers.” “I swear on my life to reach the Western Heaven,” Xuanzang responded, overwhelmed. “If not, I will never return home and instead pass straight to Hell.” The beaming emperor now returned to the palace, to prepare Xuanzang’s travel documents and await an auspicious day for his departure. Xuanzang, meanwhile, went back to his own temple, which was buzzing with the news of his pledge. “Did you really volunteer to go to the Western Heaven?” one of his disciples asked him. “The way is full of tigers, leopards, demons, and monsters, wide rivers and high mountains. Will we ever see you again?” “I have made a solemn oath,” said Xuanzang. “I must repay the emperor’s generosity by serving the country. If I fail, I will be damned to eternal perdition. Remember: The active mind conjures up demons; the stilled mind extinguishes them. I may be gone for two, three, seven years, or forever. But if the pine tree inside our gate points eastward, you’ll know that I’ll be back soon.” The next morning at court, Taizong wrote out a document describing the mission and stamped it with an imperial seal granting free passage to its bearer. “The stars are auspiciously aligned today for the start of a long journey,” the Department of Astronomy reported.
human_translations.translator_4: A thousand officials with jade at their belts walked in due order. The banners of the five guards are drawn up on either side. Holding golden gourds, Wielding battle-axes, They stand in pairs; Lamps of purple gauze, Imperial censers, Make majestic clouds. Dragons fly and phoenixes dance, Ospreys and eagles soar. True is the enlightened Son of Heaven, Good are his just and loyal ministers. This age of prosperity surpasses the time of Shun and Yu; The eternal peace he has given outdoes that of Yao and Tang. Under a parasol with curved handle The dragon robe sweeps in, Dazzling bright. Interlocking jade rings, Coloured phoenix fans, Shimmer with a magic glow. Pearl crowns and belts of jade, Gold seals on purple cords. A thousand regiments of soldiers protect the imperial chariot, Two lines of generals carry the royal chair. Bathed and reverent, the Emperor comes to worship the Buddha, Submitting to the True Achievement as he joyfully burns incense. When the carriage of the Tang Emperor reached the temple, orders were given to stop the music as he descended from the vehicle and went at the head of his officials to bow to the Buddha and burn incense. When he had done this three times he looked up and saw what a magnificent assembly it was: Dancing banners, Flying canopies. When the banners danced The sky shook with the clouds of silk; When the canopies flew The sun gleamed as the red lightning flashed. Perfect the image of the statue of the Honoured One, Mighty the grandeur of the Arhats' countenances. Magic flowers in a vase, Censers burning sandalwood and laka. As the fairy flowers stand in vases Trees like brocade fill the temple with their brightness. As the censers burn sandalwood and laka Clouds of incense rise to the azure heaven. Fresh fruit of the season is piled in vermilion dishes, Exotic sweets are heaped on the silk-covered tables. Serried ranks of holy monks intone the surras To save abandoned souls from suffering. Taizong and his civil and military officials all burned incense, bowed to the golden body of the Lord Buddha, and paid their respects to the Arhats. The Hierarch Chen Xuanzang then led all the monks to bow to the Emperor, and when this was over they divided into their groups and went to their meditation places while the Hierarch showed the Emperor the notice about the delivery of the lonely ghosts. It read: “Mysterious is the ultimate virtue, and the Sect of Meditation leads to Nirvana. The purity of the truth is all-knowing; it pervades the Three Regions of the universe. Through its countless changes it controls the Negative and Positive; unbounded are the embodiments of the eternal reality. In considering those forlorn ghosts one should be deeply distressed. At the sacred command of Taizong we have assembled some chosen monks for meditation and preaching. He has opened wide the gates of enlightenment and rowed far the boat of mercy, saving all the beings in the sea of suffering, and delivering those who had long been afflicted by the six ways of existence. They will be led back to the right road and revel in the great chaos; in action and in passivity they will be at one with primal simplicity. For this wonderful cause they are invited to see the purple gates of the pure capital, and through our assembly they will escape from the confines of Hell to climb to the World of Bliss and be free, wandering as they please in the Paradise of the West. As the poem goes: A burner of incense of longevity, A few spells to achieve rebirth. The infinite Law is proclaimed, The boundless mercy of Heaven is shown. When sins are all washed away, The neglected souls leave Hell. We pray to protect our country; May it stay at peace and be blessed.” When he had read this the Tang Emperor's heart was filled with happiness and he said to the monks, “Hold firm to your sincerity and never allow yourselves a moment's slackness in the service of the Buddha. Later on, when the Assembly is over, you will be blessed and we shall richly reward you. You shall certainly not have labored in vain.” The twelve hundred monks all kowtowed to thank him.

translation:
Thousands of officials flanked the emperor, the Five Guards' banners standing tall on either side.  He held a golden gourd, another held an axe and halberd, facing each other in a perfect pair. Crimson silk candles burned, incense burned in censers, filling the hall with an air of solemnity. Dragons soared, phoenixes flapped, eagles soared, hawks dipped.  

The enlightened and virtuous emperor stood in all his majesty, his loyal and righteous ministers surrounding him. May this fortune last for a thousand years, surpassing even Shun and Yu, may peace for ten thousand generations be like that of Yao and Tang.

Then, we saw the curved hand-grip umbrella, the dragon robe shimmering, its radiance clashing with that of the jeweled crown and jade girdle, the purple sash and gold insignia. Thousands of troops guarded the imperial procession, two lines of carriages followed. 

The emperor, bathed in a reverent devotion, meticulously bowed to Buddha, accepting the blessings of good fortune, offering incense. 

The Tang King arrived early, came before the temple, silenced the music and instruments, stepped out of his carriage, followed by many officials. Bowing, he offered incense before Buddha, performing three circumambulations. Lifting his head, he beheld a magnificent gathering. Banners swayed in the wind, treasures emitted brilliant light. 

The banners, swirling, cast dancing rainbows upon the void; the jeweled umbrellas, gleaming, reflected the sun, red light streaked across the heavens. The majestic golden image of the Buddha, the serene faces of the Arhats – all held immense power. 

Flower-filled vases graced the area, sandalwood incense filled the air.  The flowers, bright and abundant, adorned the temple; the incense, a fragrant cloud, pierced through the clear sky. New fruits, exquisitely arranged on crimson trays, sweets and pastries, piled high on colorful platforms.

High monks, their voices booming, chanted sutras, wishing to free troubled souls from suffering. The emperor, his ministers both civil and martial, offered incense, bowed to the golden body of Buddha, and meditated before the Arhats. 

Then, the great Grand Master Xuanzang, master of the Grand Chan School, led the monks in saluting the Tang King. After the ceremony, the monks dispersed and settled into meditation postures. The master presented the Emperor with a scroll inscribed with “Mercy and Compassion,” which read:

"Supreme virtue is vast, the Chan School is beyond comprehension. Purity, clarity, and insight, permeate the Three Realms. Infinite change, encompassing yin and yang.  True nature, without limit, eternally present. Seeing the plight of the lonely souls, we must feel compassion. By the Imperial decree, a gathering of monks was assembled to practice Zen and preach the Dharma.  

Opening the gates of convenience, offering a ship of mercy, to rescue all beings from suffering, to liberate them from the ailments of the Six Paths. Leading them to the true path, to enjoy the clear joys of paradise. Comprehending stillness and actionlessness, returning to original purity.

By this auspicious opportunity, invite them to the jeweled palace of the capital. Seize this favorable moment, to escape from the prison of hell and the mundane world.  Quickly ascend to the Realm of Bliss, wandering freely in the west.

Here is a poem:

A single furnace of eternal life incense,
Several scrolls of transcendence.

Boundless marvelous Dharma proclaimed,
Infinite heavenly grace received.

All grievances are erased,
All souls released from their prison.

May my kingdom and family prosper,
Enjoying a thousand years of peace."

The emperor, overjoyed, addressed the monks: "You all possess genuine devotion, do not slacken your efforts in Buddhist affairs. When the work is complete and your merits are fulfilled, each of you will receive great reward, your efforts will not be in vain."

Those twelve hundred monks, all bowed together in gratitude.
source_text: 千官环佩分前后，五卫旌旗列两旁。执金瓜，擎斧钺，双双对对；绛纱烛，御炉香，霭霭堂堂。龙飞凤舞，鹗荐鹰扬。圣明天子正，忠义大臣良。介福千年过舜禹，升平万代赛尧汤。又见那曲柄伞，滚龙袍，辉光相射；玉连环，彩凤扇，瑞霭飘扬。珠冠玉带，紫绶金章。护驾军千队，扶舆将两行。这皇帝沐浴虔诚尊敬佛，皈依善果喜拈香。唐王大驾，早到寺前，吩咐住了音乐响器，下了车辇，引着多官。拜佛拈香。三匝已毕，抬头观看，果然好座道场，但见：幢幡飘舞，宝盖飞辉。幢幡飘舞，凝空道道彩霞摇；宝盖飞辉，映日翩翩红电彻。世尊金象貌臻臻，罗汉玉容威烈烈。瓶插仙花，炉焚檀降。瓶插仙花，锦树辉辉漫宝刹；炉焚檀降，香云霭霭透清霄。时新果品砌朱盘，奇样糖酥堆彩案。高僧罗列诵真经，愿拔孤魂离苦难。太宗文武俱各拈香，拜了佛祖金身，参了罗汉。又见那大阐都纲陈玄奘法师引众僧罗拜唐王。礼毕，分班各安禅位，法师献上济孤榜文与太宗看，榜曰：“至德渺茫，禅宗寂灭。清净灵通，周流三界。千变万化，统摄阴阳。体用真常，无穷极矣。观彼孤魂，深宜哀愍。此奉太宗圣命：选集诸僧，参禅讲法。大开方便门庭，广运慈悲舟楫，普济苦海群生，脱免沉疴六趣。引归真路，普玩鸿蒙；动止无为，混成纯素。仗此良因，邀赏清都绛阙；乘吾胜会，脱离地狱凡笼。早登极乐任逍遥，来往西方随自在。诗曰：一炉永寿香，几卷超生箓。无边妙法宣，无际天恩沐。冤孽尽消除，孤魂皆出狱。愿保我邦家，清平万年福。”太宗看了满心欢喜，对众僧道：“汝等秉立丹衷，切休怠慢佛事。待后功成完备，各各福有所归，朕当重赏，决不空劳。”那一千二百僧，一齐顿首称谢。

Remember: The active mind conjures up demons; the stilled mind extinguishes them. I may be gone for two, three, seven years, or forever. But if the pine tree inside our gate points eastward, you’ll know that I’ll be back soon.” The next morning at court, Taizong wrote out a document describing the mission and stamped it with an imperial seal granting free passage to its bearer. “The stars are auspiciously aligned today for the start of a long journey,” the Department of Astronomy reported.
human_translations.translator_4: A thousand officials with jade at their belts walked in due order. The banners of the five guards are drawn up on either side. Holding golden gourds, Wielding battle-axes, They stand in pairs; Lamps of purple gauze, Imperial censers, Make majestic clouds. Dragons fly and phoenixes dance, Ospreys and eagles soar. True is the enlightened Son of Heaven, Good are his just and loyal ministers. This age of prosperity surpasses the time of Shun and Yu; The eternal peace he has given outdoes that of Yao and Tang. Under a parasol with curved handle The dragon robe sweeps in, Dazzling bright. Interlocking jade rings, Coloured phoenix fans, Shimmer with a magic glow. Pearl crowns and belts of jade, Gold seals on purple cords. A thousand regiments of soldiers protect the imperial chariot, Two lines of generals carry the royal chair. Bathed and reverent, the Emperor comes to worship the Buddha, Submitting to the True Achievement as he joyfully burns incense. When the carriage of the Tang Emperor reached the temple, orders were given to stop the music as he descended from the vehicle and went at the head of his officials to bow to the Buddha and burn incense. When he had done this three times he looked up and saw what a magnificent assembly it was: Dancing banners, Flying canopies. When the banners danced The sky shook with the clouds of silk; When the canopies flew The sun gleamed as the red lightning flashed. Perfect the image of the statue of the Honoured One, Mighty the grandeur of the Arhats' countenances. Magic flowers in a vase, Censers burning sandalwood and laka. As the fairy flowers stand in vases Trees like brocade fill the temple with their brightness. As the censers burn sandalwood and laka Clouds of incense rise to the azure heaven. Fresh fruit of the season is piled in vermilion dishes, Exotic sweets are heaped on the silk-covered tables. Serried ranks of holy monks intone the surras To save abandoned souls from suffering. Taizong and his civil and military officials all burned incense, bowed to the golden body of the Lord Buddha, and paid their respects to the Arhats. The Hierarch Chen Xuanzang then led all the monks to bow to the Emperor, and when this was over they divided into their groups and went to their meditation places while the Hierarch showed the Emperor the notice about the delivery of the lonely ghosts. It read: “Mysterious is the ultimate virtue, and the Sect of Meditation leads to Nirvana. The purity of the truth is all-knowing; it pervades the Three Regions of the universe. Through its countless changes it controls the Negative and Positive; unbounded are the embodiments of the eternal reality. In considering those forlorn ghosts one should be deeply distressed. At the sacred command of Taizong we have assembled some chosen monks for meditation and preaching. He has opened wide the gates of enlightenment and rowed far the boat of mercy, saving all the beings in the sea of suffering, and delivering those who had long been afflicted by the six ways of existence. They will be led back to the right road and revel in the great chaos; in action and in passivity they will be at one with primal simplicity. For this wonderful cause they are invited to see the purple gates of the pure capital, and through our assembly they will escape from the confines of Hell to climb to the World of Bliss and be free, wandering as they please in the Paradise of the West. As the poem goes: A burner of incense of longevity, A few spells to achieve rebirth. The infinite Law is proclaimed, The boundless mercy of Heaven is shown. When sins are all washed away, The neglected souls leave Hell. We pray to protect our country; May it stay at peace and be blessed.” When he had read this the Tang Emperor's heart was filled with happiness and he said to the monks, “Hold firm to your sincerity and never allow yourselves a moment's slackness in the service of the Buddha. translation:
Thousands of officials surrounded the imperial procession, the five armies' banners stood in two lines on either side. Holding golden gourds, brandishing axes and halberds, they stood in pairs; crimson silk candles illuminated the imperial furnace, emitting a fragrant smoke, filling the hall with grandeur. Dragons and phoenixes danced, eagles soared, falcons dived. The emperor, virtuous and upright, was bathed in the light of heaven. Loyal and virtuous ministers surrounded him. His merits surpassed those of Shun and Yu, and his reign would be as glorious as that of Yao and Tang.

We see the ornate scepter-handle umbrella, the dragon robe shining with splendor, and the magnificent lights reflected in each other.  Jade necklaces, colorful peacock fans, and auspicious clouds billowed. A crown of jewels and a belt of jade, purple sashes and gold decorations adorned him. Thousand-strong guards of honor lined the procession, palanquin bearers walked in two rows. The emperor, devout and respectful, bathed in the divine light, embraced the fruit of Buddha, and joyously offered incense. 

King Tang arrived early, before the temple, ordered the musical instruments silenced, stepped down from his palanquin, and led his many officials. He bowed and offered incense. After three circuits, he looked up and saw that this truly was a magnificent temple. Banners fluttered in the wind, and the jeweled parasol shimmered.  The banners danced, painting the sky with swirling clouds of colorful light; the jeweled parasol shone, reflecting the sun, sending ripples of red light through the heavens. The Buddha's golden figure, majestic and lifelike, the arhats, with their jade faces, radiated power.  

Vases filled with immortal flowers, sandalwood incense burning, a perfect picture. Vases filled with immortal flowers, glittering tree branches illuminated the magnificent temple; sandalwood incense burning, sending fragrant clouds rising through the clear sky. 

Fresh fruits piled on vermilion platters, peculiar sweets and pastries arranged on colorful trays.  High monks sat in rows, reciting scriptures, hoping to free lonely souls from suffering. Emperor Taizong, both civil and military officials, offered incense and bowed to the Buddha's golden body, and paid respects to the arhats.  We then see the high priest Xuanzang, leading the gathered monks, bowing to Emperor Tang. After the ceremony, they took their places, and the high priest presented Emperor Taizong with a scroll inscribed with the "Rescue of Souls."  The scroll read: "Great virtue is vast and boundless, the Zen school has reached its peak. Pure and intelligent, flowing through the three realms. Changes and transformations abound, encompassing yin and yang. True essence in form and function, endless and immeasurable. Seeing these lonely souls, one should surely pity them deeply.  By imperial decree, I, the emperor, have selected these monks to practice Zen and teach the Dharma. To open a wide gate of convenience, to navigate the ship of compassion, to liberate all living beings in the sea of suffering, to free them from the pain of the six realms. Guide them to the true path, to savor the great primordial chaos; stillness and action, effortless, united in pure existence.  

Relying on this excellent opportunity, let us appreciate the clear capital and the magnificent purple palace; at this auspicious gathering, escape the hells and mortal realms. Ascend to paradise and enjoy eternal bliss, coming and going freely to the West. The poem says:
A furnace of everlasting incense,
A few scrolls of transcendence.
Boundless Dharma proclaimed,
Unlimited heavenly grace.
All grievances dispelled,
Lonely souls freed from prison. 
May this land flourish,
A thousand years of peace and blessings.”

Emperor Taizong read it with great joy and told the monks, "You all possess a sincere heart, do not neglect the Buddha's affairs. When your efforts are complete, and each of you achieves great merit, I will reward you accordingly, never leaving you unrewarded.”

The one thousand two hundred monks all bowed their heads in unison, expressing their gratitude.
source_text: 千官环佩分前后，五卫旌旗列两旁。执金瓜，擎斧钺，双双对对；绛纱烛，御炉香，霭霭堂堂。龙飞凤舞，鹗荐鹰扬。圣明天子正，忠义大臣良。介福千年过舜禹，升平万代赛尧汤。又见那曲柄伞，滚龙袍，辉光相射；玉连环，彩凤扇，瑞霭飘扬。珠冠玉带，紫绶金章。护驾军千队，扶舆将两行。这皇帝沐浴虔诚尊敬佛，皈依善果喜拈香。唐王大驾，早到寺前，吩咐住了音乐响器，下了车辇，引着多官。拜佛拈香。三匝已毕，抬头观看，果然好座道场，但见：幢幡飘舞，宝盖飞辉。幢幡飘舞，凝空道道彩霞摇；宝盖飞辉，映日翩翩红电彻。世尊金象貌臻臻，罗汉玉容威烈烈。瓶插仙花，炉焚檀降。瓶插仙花，锦树辉辉漫宝刹；炉焚檀降，香云霭霭透清霄。时新果品砌朱盘，奇样糖酥堆彩案。高僧罗列诵真经，愿拔孤魂离苦难。太宗文武俱各拈香，拜了佛祖金身，参了罗汉。又见那大阐都纲陈玄奘法师引众僧罗拜唐王。礼毕，分班各安禅位，法师献上济孤榜文与太宗看，榜曰：“至德渺茫，禅宗寂灭。清净灵通，周流三界。千变万化，统摄阴阳。体用真常，无穷极矣。观彼孤魂，深宜哀愍。此奉太宗圣命：选集诸僧，参禅讲法。大开方便门庭，广运慈悲舟楫，普济苦海群生，脱免沉疴六趣。引归真路，普玩鸿蒙；动止无为，混成纯素。仗此良因，邀赏清都绛阙；乘吾胜会，脱离地狱凡笼。早登极乐任逍遥，来往西方随自在。诗曰：一炉永寿香，几卷超生箓。无边妙法宣，无际天恩沐。冤孽尽消除，孤魂皆出狱。愿保我邦家，清平万年福。”太宗看了满心欢喜，对众僧道：“汝等秉立丹衷，切休怠慢佛事。待后功成完备，各各福有所归，朕当重赏，决不空劳。”那一千二百僧，一齐顿首称谢。

human_translations.translator_1: A thousand lords with girdle-jade walk in front and rear. The many flags of guardsmen stand both left and right. Those holding gilt bludgeons, And halberds and axes, March in pairs and pairs; The red silk lanterns, The royal incense urn, Move in solemnity. The dragons fly and the phoenixes dance; The falcons soar and the eagles take wing. This Son of Heaven’s an upright sage; The righteous ministers are good. They increase our bliss by a thousand years, surpassing Yu and Shun; They secure peace of ten thousand ages, rivaling Yao and Tang. We also see the curve-handled umbrella, And robes with rolling dragons— Their glare lighting up each other; The jade joined-rings, The phoenix fans, Waving through holy mist. Those caps of pearls and belts of jade; The purple sashes and medals of gold. A thousand rows of soldiers protect the Throne; Two lines of marshals uphold the carriage. This emperor, cleansed and sincere, bows to the Buddha, Glad to raise incense and seek virtue’s fruit. The grand cortege of the Tang emperor soon arrived in front of the temple. The emperor ordered a halt to the music, left the carriages, and led many officials in the worship of Buddha by taking up burning incense sticks in their hands. After bowing three times holding the incense, they raised their heads and looked around them. This was indeed a splendid religious hall. You see Dancing flags and banners; Bright, gleaming sunshades. Dancing flags and banners Fill the air with strands of flashing colored mists. Bright, gleaming sunshades Glow in the sun as fiery bolts. Imposing, the gold image of Lokājyeṣṭha;14 Most awesome, the jade features of the arhats. Divine flowers fill the vases. Sandalwood incense burn in the urns. The divine flowers filling the vases Adorn the temple with a brilliant forest of brocade. The sandalwood incense burning in the urns Covers the clear sky with waves of fragrant clouds. Piled high on red trays are fruits in season. On colored counters, mounds of cakes and sweets rest. Rows of noble priests chant the holy sūtras To save from their travails those orphaned souls. Taizong and his officials each lifted the incense; they also worshipped the golden body of the Buddha and paid homage to the arhats. Thereafter, the Master of the Law, Chen Xuanzang, the Grand Expositor of the Faith, led the various monks to greet the Tang emperor. After the ceremony, they went back to their seats according to their rank and station. The priest then presented Taizong with the proclamation for the deliverance of the orphaned souls. It read: The supreme virtue is vast and endless, for Buddhism is founded upon Nirvāṇa. The spirit of the pure and the clean circulates freely and flows everywhere in the Three Regions. There are a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations, all regulated by the forces of yin and yang. Boundless and vast indeed are the substance, the function, the true nature, and the permanence of such phenomena. But look at those orphaned souls, how worthy they are of our pity and commiseration! Now by the holy command of Taizong, we have selected and assembled various priests, who will engage in meditation and in the proclamation of the Law. Flinging wide the gates of salvation and setting in motion many vessels of mercy, we would deliver you, the multitudes, from the Sea of Woe and save you from perdition and from the Sixfold Path. You will be led to return to the way of truth and to enjoy the bliss of Heaven. Whether it be by motion, rest, or nonactivity, you will be united with, and become, pure essences. Therefore make use of this noble occasion, for you are invited to the pleasures of the celestial city. Take advantage of our Grand Mass so that you may find release from Hell’s confinement, ascend quickly and freely to ultimate bliss, and travel without restraint in the Region of the West.15 The poem says: An urn of immortal incense. Some scrolls of salvific power. As we proclaim this boundless Law, Receive now Heaven’s endless grace. All your guilt and crime abolished, You lost souls may leave your prison. May our nation be firmly blessed With peace long and all-embracing. Highly pleased by what he read, Taizong said to the monks, “Be firm, all of you, in your devotion, and do not slack in your service to Buddha. After the achievement of merit and after each has received his blessing, we shall reward you handsomely. Be assured that you will not have labored in vain.”
human_translations.translator_2: There was no thunder and no lightning after this. This made the Wizard still more anxious, and he burnt more incense and charms and recited more incantations and struck the table as his fourth signal. Instantly the dragons from the four oceans appeared. Sun cried out above their heads, “Aoguang, where do you think you are going?” Aoguang and his companions came forward and bowed. Then Sun told them what he had told the other helpers before, and added, “You helped me before though not successfully. Today I hope you will help me with success.” The Dragon King replied, “I gladly obey your orders.” Sun said, “I beg of you to give me a helping hand. The Wizard’s signal of the fourth performance is now finished. It is now my turn, and I expect you all to help me. I burn no incense and have no signal but my club. When I lift up my spear the first time, I want the wind to blow.” The Mistress of the Wind said, “The wind shall blow.” “When I lift up my spear the second time, I want the clouds to gather.” The Master of the Clouds said, “The clouds shall gather.” “When I lift up my spear the third time, I want thunder and lightning.” The Master of Thunder and Mistress of Lightning said, “You shall have them in abundance.” “When I lift up my spear the fourth time, I want rain.” The Dragon replied, “Your orders shall be obeyed.” “When I lift up my spear the fifth time, I want a clear sky without fail.” Having arranged this, he restored the false Sun and took his place. He shouted out, “Master Wizard, your fourth signal for performance is now over and there has been neither wind, clouds, thunder, lightning, nor rain. Now it is my time to try.” The Wizard came down from his platform altar and went to the gallery by the king, and the Monkey followed him. The king asked the wizard how it was that none of his four attempts were successful. The wizard replied, “The rain king was not at home today.” The Monkey angrily replied, “The dragon gods were all at home, but your Royal Wizard is not sufficiently skilful.” The king then ordered the Buddhist monks to mount the platform. Sun invited the Master to go, but he said he could not command rain.
human_translations.translator_3: “How wonderful!” gasped all present—including the emperor—kneeling, bowing, and burning incense. Taizong called quickly for a skilled painter to sketch a true likeness of the Bodhisattva, but as soon as the artist lifted his brush, the vision vaporized, leaving only a slip of paper drifting down on the breeze. On it was written the following message: Greetings, Emperor of the Tang! 108,000 miles west of here, wonderful texts speak of the Mahayana. Once distributed throughout your empire, these sutras will deliver the ghosts of the damned from Hell. He who is willing to seek them will become a golden Buddha. “Let’s pause the mass and our pursuit of virtue until someone has brought back these miraculous scriptures,” decided the emperor. “But who will go?” asked his officials. “Though entirely useless,” Xuanzang instantly spoke up, “I volunteer to fetch these treasures that will secure the empire in perpetuity.” The emperor immediately raised Xuanzang to his feet and bowed four times to him. “For such sacrifice and service, we will become brothers.” “I swear on my life to reach the Western Heaven,” Xuanzang responded, overwhelmed. “If not, I will never return home and instead pass straight to Hell.” The beaming emperor now returned to the palace, to prepare Xuanzang’s travel documents and await an auspicious day for his departure. Xuanzang, meanwhile, went back to his own temple, which was buzzing with the news of his pledge. “Did you really volunteer to go to the Western Heaven?” one of his disciples asked him. “The way is full of tigers, leopards, demons, and monsters, wide rivers and high mountains. Will we ever see you again?” “I have made a solemn oath,” said Xuanzang. “I must repay the emperor’s generosity by serving the country. If I fail, I will be damned to eternal perdition. Remember: The active mind conjures up demons; the stilled mind extinguishes them. I may be gone for two, three, seven years, or forever. But if the pine tree inside our gate points eastward, you’ll know that I’ll be back soon.” The next morning at court, Taizong wrote out a document describing the mission and stamped it with an imperial seal granting free passage to its bearer. “The stars are auspiciously aligned today for the start of a long journey,” the Department of Astronomy reported.

translation:
Thousands of officials surround the emperor, their belts adorned with jeweled ornaments, while five guards stand in formation on either side. One holds a golden mallet, the other an axe; the two stand in unison.

Red silk candles illuminate the room, incense from a burning brazier fills the air, creating an atmosphere of grandeur. Dragons and phoenixes dance, hawks and eagles soar. The holy sovereign, the enlightened emperor, is present; his loyal ministers are righteous. He surpasses the virtues of Yao and Shun by a thousand years, surpassing the peace of Yu and Tang by ten thousand.

And there, the emperor's staff shines, reflecting the brilliance of his dragon-emblazoned robe. Jade rings and a fan decorated with colorful phoenixes radiate auspiciousness. His jeweled crown, jade belt, purple sash, and gold insignia gleam. A thousand troops of imperial guards surround him, two lines of palanquin bearers follow close behind. The emperor, in a reverent and pious manner, bathes in the light of the Buddha, joyfully accepting the merit of incense offerings.

King Tang arrives early, approaches the temple, commands the musical instruments to be silenced, disembarks from his carriage, and leads his entourage of officials to bow before the Buddha, offering incense.

After three turns, he raises his head to gaze upon the magnificent temple. He sees banners fluttering, jeweled canopies radiating brilliance. The banners flutter and dance, painting the sky with colored clouds; the canopies shine, reflecting the sun's rays like crimson lightning. The Buddha's golden elephant form is truly magnificent, the Arhat's jade faces radiate a powerful aura. 

Fresh fruits are arranged on a red platter, exotic sweets piled high on a colorful tray. High monks recite the true sutras, wishing to free lonely souls from their suffering.

Emperor Taizong, both civil and military officials, light incense, bow before the Buddha's golden form, and venerate the Arhats. 

Master Xuanzang, the Grand Abbot of the Eastern Capital Temple, leads the monks in a respectful bow to King Tang.

Upon completing the ceremony, the monks take their assigned meditation positions. Master Xuanzang presents Emperor Taizong with a scroll bearing the inscription: "Great virtue is vast and boundless, the Chan school is silent and profound. Purity and clarity pervade all realms.  Transformations are endless, encompassing yin and yang. Their function is eternal, boundless and supreme. Observe the lonely souls, deeply worthy of compassion. 

This is in response to Emperor Taizong's sacred decree: 

Selected monks have been gathered, Chan meditation and teachings are given. The doors of convenience are wide open, the vessel of compassion is readily available. All beings suffering in the ocean of Samsara are liberated from their ailments and released from their six realms of existence. They are guided back to the true path, the primordial chaos. Rest and stillness without action, merging into pure essence. 

Relying on this good cause, we invite all to behold the clear city of the Purple Palace. Utilize this auspicious gathering, escape from the prisons of hell and the mortal realm. Ascend to the realm of bliss and freedom, come and go in the West as you please.

Poetry states: 

One furnace of eternal incense, countless scrolls of liberation. 

Boundless wonders of dharma proclaimed, boundless grace of heaven received. 

All karmic debts are extinguished, all lonely souls are freed from captivity. 

May the blessings of my kingdom be forever peaceful, for ten thousand years of prosperity."

Upon reading this, Emperor Taizong is filled with joy. He turns to the monks and says, "May you all uphold your sincere intentions and never neglect Buddhist matters. After your tasks are complete and all have attained their blessings, I will generously reward you and ensure that your efforts are not in vain."

The 1,200 monks all bow their heads in unison and express their gratitude.
source_text: 千官环佩分前后，五卫旌旗列两旁。执金瓜，擎斧钺，双双对对；绛纱烛，御炉香，霭霭堂堂。龙飞凤舞，鹗荐鹰扬。圣明天子正，忠义大臣良。介福千年过舜禹，升平万代赛尧汤。又见那曲柄伞，滚龙袍，辉光相射；玉连环，彩凤扇，瑞霭飘扬。珠冠玉带，紫绶金章。护驾军千队，扶舆将两行。这皇帝沐浴虔诚尊敬佛，皈依善果喜拈香。唐王大驾，早到寺前，吩咐住了音乐响器，下了车辇，引着多官。拜佛拈香。三匝已毕，抬头观看，果然好座道场，但见：幢幡飘舞，宝盖飞辉。幢幡飘舞，凝空道道彩霞摇；宝盖飞辉，映日翩翩红电彻。世尊金象貌臻臻，罗汉玉容威烈烈。瓶插仙花，炉焚檀降。瓶插仙花，锦树辉辉漫宝刹；炉焚檀降，香云霭霭透清霄。时新果品砌朱盘，奇样糖酥堆彩案。高僧罗列诵真经，愿拔孤魂离苦难。太宗文武俱各拈香，拜了佛祖金身，参了罗汉。又见那大阐都纲陈玄奘法师引众僧罗拜唐王。礼毕，分班各安禅位，法师献上济孤榜文与太宗看，榜曰：“至德渺茫，禅宗寂灭。清净灵通，周流三界。千变万化，统摄阴阳。体用真常，无穷极矣。观彼孤魂，深宜哀愍。此奉太宗圣命：选集诸僧，参禅讲法。大开方便门庭，广运慈悲舟楫，普济苦海群生，脱免沉疴六趣。引归真路，普玩鸿蒙；动止无为，混成纯素。仗此良因，邀赏清都绛阙；乘吾胜会，脱离地狱凡笼。早登极乐任逍遥，来往西方随自在。诗曰：一炉永寿香，几卷超生箓。无边妙法宣，无际天恩沐。冤孽尽消除，孤魂皆出狱。愿保我邦家，清平万年福。”太宗看了满心欢喜，对众僧道：“汝等秉立丹衷，切休怠慢佛事。待后功成完备，各各福有所归，朕当重赏，决不空劳。”那一千二百僧，一齐顿首称谢。

human_translations.translator_1: A thousand lords with girdle-jade walk in front and rear. The many flags of guardsmen stand both left and right. Those holding gilt bludgeons, And halberds and axes, March in pairs and pairs; The red silk lanterns, The royal incense urn, Move in solemnity. The dragons fly and the phoenixes dance; The falcons soar and the eagles take wing. This Son of Heaven’s an upright sage; The righteous ministers are good. They increase our bliss by a thousand years, surpassing Yu and Shun; They secure peace of ten thousand ages, rivaling Yao and Tang. We also see the curve-handled umbrella, And robes with rolling dragons— Their glare lighting up each other; The jade joined-rings, The phoenix fans, Waving through holy mist. Those caps of pearls and belts of jade; The purple sashes and medals of gold. A thousand rows of soldiers protect the Throne; Two lines of marshals uphold the carriage. This emperor, cleansed and sincere, bows to the Buddha, Glad to raise incense and seek virtue’s fruit. The grand cortege of the Tang emperor soon arrived in front of the temple. The emperor ordered a halt to the music, left the carriages, and led many officials in the worship of Buddha by taking up burning incense sticks in their hands. After bowing three times holding the incense, they raised their heads and looked around them. This was indeed a splendid religious hall. You see Dancing flags and banners; Bright, gleaming sunshades. Dancing flags and banners Fill the air with strands of flashing colored mists. Bright, gleaming sunshades Glow in the sun as fiery bolts. Imposing, the gold image of Lokājyeṣṭha;14 Most awesome, the jade features of the arhats. Divine flowers fill the vases. Sandalwood incense burn in the urns. The divine flowers filling the vases Adorn the temple with a brilliant forest of brocade. The sandalwood incense burning in the urns Covers the clear sky with waves of fragrant clouds. Piled high on red trays are fruits in season. On colored counters, mounds of cakes and sweets rest. Rows of noble priests chant the holy sūtras To save from their travails those orphaned souls. Taizong and his officials each lifted the incense; they also worshipped the golden body of the Buddha and paid homage to the arhats. Thereafter, the Master of the Law, Chen Xuanzang, the Grand Expositor of the Faith, led the various monks to greet the Tang emperor. After the ceremony, they went back to their seats according to their rank and station. The priest then presented Taizong with the proclamation for the deliverance of the orphaned souls. It read: The supreme virtue is vast and endless, for Buddhism is founded upon Nirvāṇa. The spirit of the pure and the clean circulates freely and flows everywhere in the Three Regions. There are a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations, all regulated by the forces of yin and yang. Boundless and vast indeed are the substance, the function, the true nature, and the permanence of such phenomena. But look at those orphaned souls, how worthy they are of our pity and commiseration! Now by the holy command of Taizong, we have selected and assembled various priests, who will engage in meditation and in the proclamation of the Law. Flinging wide the gates of salvation and setting in motion many vessels of mercy, we would deliver you, the multitudes, from the Sea of Woe and save you from perdition and from the Sixfold Path. You will be led to return to the way of truth and to enjoy the bliss of Heaven. Whether it be by motion, rest, or nonactivity, you will be united with, and become, pure essences. Therefore make use of this noble occasion, for you are invited to the pleasures of the celestial city. Take advantage of our Grand Mass so that you may find release from Hell’s confinement, ascend quickly and freely to ultimate bliss, and travel without restraint in the Region of the West.15 The poem says: An urn of immortal incense. Some scrolls of salvific power. As we proclaim this boundless Law, Receive now Heaven’s endless grace. All your guilt and crime abolished, You lost souls may leave your prison. May our nation be firmly blessed With peace long and all-embracing. Highly pleased by what he read, Taizong said to the monks, “Be firm, all of you, in your devotion, and do not slack in your service to Buddha. After the achievement of merit and after each has received his blessing, we shall reward you handsomely. Be assured that you will not have labored in vain.”
human_translations.translator_2: There was no thunder and no lightning after this. This made the Wizard still more anxious, and he burnt more incense and charms and recited more incantations and struck the table as his fourth signal. Instantly the dragons from the four oceans appeared. Sun cried out above their heads, “Aoguang, where do you think you are going?” Aoguang and his companions came forward and bowed. Then Sun told them what he had told the other helpers before, and added, “You helped me before though not successfully. Today I hope you will help me with success.” The Dragon King replied, “I gladly obey your orders.” Sun said, “I beg of you to give me a helping hand. The Wizard’s signal of the fourth performance is now finished. It is now my turn, and I expect you all to help me. I burn no incense and have no signal but my club. When I lift up my spear the first time, I want the wind to blow.” The Mistress of the Wind said, “The wind shall blow.” “When I lift up my spear the second time, I want the clouds to gather.” The Master of the Clouds said, “The clouds shall gather.” “When I lift up my spear the third time, I want thunder and lightning.” The Master of Thunder and Mistress of Lightning said, “You shall have them in abundance.” “When I lift up my spear the fourth time, I want rain.” The Dragon replied, “Your orders shall be obeyed.” “When I lift up my spear the fifth time, I want a clear sky without fail.” Having arranged this, he restored the false Sun and took his place. He shouted out, “Master Wizard, your fourth signal for performance is now over and there has been neither wind, clouds, thunder, lightning, nor rain. Now it is my time to try.” The Wizard came down from his platform altar and went to the gallery by the king, and the Monkey followed him. The king asked the wizard how it was that none of his four attempts were successful. The wizard replied, “The rain king was not at home today.” The Monkey angrily replied, “The dragon gods were all at home, but your Royal Wizard is not sufficiently skilful.” The king then ordered the Buddhist monks to mount the platform. Sun invited the Master to go, but he said he could not command rain.
human_translations.translator_3: “How wonderful!” gasped all present—including the emperor—kneeling, bowing, and burning incense. Taizong called quickly for a skilled painter to sketch a true likeness of the Bodhisattva, but as soon as the artist lifted his brush, the vision vaporized, leaving only a slip of paper drifting down on the breeze. On it was written the following message: Greetings, Emperor of the Tang! 108,000 miles west of here, wonderful texts speak of the Mahayana. Once distributed throughout your empire, these sutras will deliver the ghosts of the damned from Hell. He who is willing to seek them will become a golden Buddha. “Let’s pause the mass and our pursuit of virtue until someone has brought back these miraculous scriptures,” decided the emperor. “But who will go?” asked his officials. “Though entirely useless,” Xuanzang instantly spoke up, “I volunteer to fetch these treasures that will secure the empire in perpetuity.” The emperor immediately raised Xuanzang to his feet and bowed four times to him. “For such sacrifice and service, we will become brothers.” “I swear on my life to reach the Western Heaven,” Xuanzang responded, overwhelmed. “If not, I will never return home and instead pass straight to Hell.” The beaming emperor now returned to the palace, to prepare Xuanzang’s travel documents and await an auspicious day for his departure. Xuanzang, meanwhile, went back to his own temple, which was buzzing with the news of his pledge. “Did you really volunteer to go to the Western Heaven?” one of his disciples asked him. “The way is full of tigers, leopards, demons, and monsters, wide rivers and high mountains. Will we ever see you again?” “I have made a solemn oath,” said Xuanzang. “I must repay the emperor’s generosity by serving the country. If I fail, I will be damned to eternal perdition. Remember: The active mind conjures up demons; the stilled mind extinguishes them. I may be gone for two, three, seven years, or forever. But if the pine tree inside our gate points eastward, you’ll know that I’ll be back soon.” The next morning at court, Taizong wrote out a document describing the mission and stamped it with an imperial seal granting free passage to its bearer. “The stars are auspiciously aligned today for the start of a long journey,” the Department of Astronomy reported.

True is the enlightened Son of Heaven, Good are his just and loyal ministers. This age of prosperity surpasses the time of Shun and Yu; The eternal peace he has given outdoes that of Yao and Tang. Under a parasol with curved handle The dragon robe sweeps in, Dazzling bright. Interlocking jade rings, Coloured phoenix fans, Shimmer with a magic glow. Pearl crowns and belts of jade, Gold seals on purple cords. A thousand regiments of soldiers protect the imperial chariot, Two lines of generals carry the royal chair. Bathed and reverent, the Emperor comes to worship the Buddha, Submitting to the True Achievement as he joyfully burns incense. When the carriage of the Tang Emperor reached the temple, orders were given to stop the music as he descended from the vehicle and went at the head of his officials to bow to the Buddha and burn incense. When he had done this three times he looked up and saw what a magnificent assembly it was: Dancing banners, Flying canopies. When the banners danced The sky shook with the clouds of silk; When the canopies flew The sun gleamed as the red lightning flashed. Perfect the image of the statue of the Honoured One, Mighty the grandeur of the Arhats' countenances. Magic flowers in a vase, Censers burning sandalwood and laka. As the fairy flowers stand in vases Trees like brocade fill the temple with their brightness. As the censers burn sandalwood and laka Clouds of incense rise to the azure heaven. Fresh fruit of the season is piled in vermilion dishes, Exotic sweets are heaped on the silk-covered tables. Serried ranks of holy monks intone the surras To save abandoned souls from suffering. Taizong and his civil and military officials all burned incense, bowed to the golden body of the Lord Buddha, and paid their respects to the Arhats. The Hierarch Chen Xuanzang then led all the monks to bow to the Emperor, and when this was over they divided into their groups and went to their meditation places while the Hierarch showed the Emperor the notice about the delivery of the lonely ghosts. It read: “Mysterious is the ultimate virtue, and the Sect of Meditation leads to Nirvana. The purity of the truth is all-knowing; it pervades the Three Regions of the universe. Through its countless changes it controls the Negative and Positive; unbounded are the embodiments of the eternal reality. In considering those forlorn ghosts one should be deeply distressed. At the sacred command of Taizong we have assembled some chosen monks for meditation and preaching. He has opened wide the gates of enlightenment and rowed far the boat of mercy, saving all the beings in the sea of suffering, and delivering those who had long been afflicted by the six ways of existence. They will be led back to the right road and revel in the great chaos; in action and in passivity they will be at one with primal simplicity. For this wonderful cause they are invited to see the purple gates of the pure capital, and through our assembly they will escape from the confines of Hell to climb to the World of Bliss and be free, wandering as they please in the Paradise of the West. As the poem goes: A burner of incense of longevity, A few spells to achieve rebirth. The infinite Law is proclaimed, The boundless mercy of Heaven is shown. When sins are all washed away, The neglected souls leave Hell. We pray to protect our country; May it stay at peace and be blessed.” When he had read this the Tang Emperor's heart was filled with happiness and he said to the monks, “Hold firm to your sincerity and never allow yourselves a moment's slackness in the service of the Buddha. Later on, when the Assembly is over, you will be blessed and we shall richly reward you. You shall certainly not have labored in vain.” The twelve hundred monks all kowtowed to thank him.

translation:
"So let her be your beloved then," said Leni, "You wouldn't miss her very much if you lost her, or exchanged her for someone else, say, for me."

"Certainly," said K. smiling, "that's conceivable, but she has one great advantage over you, she knows nothing of my trial, and even if she did, she wouldn't think about it. She wouldn't try to persuade me to be more accommodating."

"That's no advantage," said Leni. "If she has no other advantages, I won't lose heart. Does she have any physical flaw?"

"A physical flaw?" asked K.

"Yes," said Leni, "I have a small one, see." She spread her middle and ring finger of her right hand apart, between which the webbing stretched almost to the top joint of the short finger. K. couldn't make out in the dark what she wanted to show him, so she guided his hand towards it.

"What a curious quirk of nature," said K., and adding, as he took in the whole hand, "What a pretty claw!"

With a certain pride, Leni watched as K., full of wonder, repeatedly spread and closed her two fingers, until he finally kissed them fleetingly and let go.

"Oh!" she exclaimed, "You kissed me!" Eagerly, with her mouth open, she climbed onto his lap with her knees. K. looked at her almost in alarm, now that she was so close, a bitter, pungent smell like pepper emanated from her, she took his head, leaned over him, and bit and kissed his neck, even biting into his hair.

"You've exchanged me!" she cried from time to time, "See, now you've exchanged me!"

Suddenly her knee slipped, and with a little cry she almost fell onto the rug. K. grasped her to keep her from falling and was pulled down towards her.

"Now you belong to me," she said.

Sie würde mich nicht zur Nachgiebigkeit zu überreden suchen.« »Das ist kein Vorteil«, sagte Leni. »Wenn sie keine sonstigen Vorteile hat, verliere ich nicht den Mut. Hat sie irgendeinen körperlichen Fehler?« »Einen körperlichen Fehler?« fragte K. »Ja«, sagte Leni, »ich habe nämlich einen solchen kleinen Fehler, sehen Sie.« Sie spannte den Mittel- und Ringfinger ihrer rechten Hand auseinander, zwischen denen das Verbindungshäutchen fast bis zum obersten Gelenk der kurzen Finger reichte. K. merkte im Dunkel nicht gleich, was sie ihm zeigen wollte, sie führte deshalb seine Hand hin, damit er es abtaste. »Was für ein Naturspiel«, sagte K. und fügte, als er die ganze Hand überblickt hatte, hinzu: »Was für eine hübsche Kralle!« Mit einer Art Stolz sah Leni zu, wie K. staunend immer wieder ihre zwei Finger auseinanderzog und zusammenlegte, bis er sie schließlich flüchtig küßte und losließ. »Oh!« rief sie aber sofort, »Sie haben mich geküßt!« Eilig, mit offenem Mund erkletterte sie mit den Knien seinen Schoß. K. sah fast bestürzt zu ihr auf, jetzt, da sie ihm so nahe war, ging ein bitterer, aufreizender Geruch wie von Pfeffer von ihr aus, sie nahm seinen Kopf an sich, beugte sich über ihn hinweg und biß und küßte seinen Hals, biß selbst in seine Haare. »Sie haben mich eingetauscht!« rief sie von Zeit zu Zeit, »sehen Sie, nun haben Sie mich eingetauscht!« Da glitt ihr Knie aus, mit einem kleinen Schrei fiel sie fast auf den Teppich, K. umfaßte sie, um sie noch zu halten, und wurde zu ihr hinabgezogen. »Jetzt gehörst du mir«, sagte sie.

translation:
“So, let her be your beloved then,” said Leni, “you wouldn’t miss her much if you lost her or exchanged her for someone else, say for me.”
“Certainly,” said K., smiling, “that’s conceivable, but she has a big advantage over you: she knows nothing about my trial, and even if she did, she wouldn’t think about it. She wouldn’t try to persuade me to be more pliable.”
“That’s not an advantage,” said Leni. “If she has no other advantages, I won’t lose heart. Does she have any physical flaws?”
“A physical flaw?” asked K.
“Yes,” said Leni, “I, for example, have such a small one, see.” She spread her middle and ring finger of her right hand apart, the webbing between them reaching almost to the top joint of the shorter finger.
K. didn’t immediately realize what she was showing him in the darkness, so she guided his hand to feel it.
“What a natural curiosity,” said K., and, after he had surveyed the whole hand, added, “What a lovely claw!”
With a kind of pride, Leni watched as K. stared, repeatedly pulling her two fingers apart and bringing them together, until he finally kissed them fleetingly and let go. 
“Oh!” she exclaimed, “You kissed me!”  Quickly, with her mouth open, she climbed onto his lap, knees bent. K. looked up at her almost in alarm; now that she was so close, a bitter, pungent smell like pepper emanated from her. She took his head in her hands, leaned over him, and bit and kissed his neck, even biting his hair.
“You’ve traded me!” she cried from time to time, “see, now you’ve traded me!”
Then her knee slipped, and with a small cry she almost fell onto the carpet. K. clasped her, to keep her from falling, and was pulled down with her. 
“Now you belong to me,” she said.

"What a quirk of nature," said K., and adding, after he had surveyed her whole hand, "What a pretty claw!" With a kind of pride, Leni watched as K. stared in wonder, repeatedly spreading and closing her two fingers, until he finally kissed them briefly and let go. "Oh!" she exclaimed, "You kissed me!" Eagerly, with her mouth open, she climbed onto his lap, her knees pressed against him. K. looked at her almost in alarm; now that she was so close, a bitter, irritating smell, like pepper, emanated from her. She took his head in her hands, bent over him, and bit and kissed his neck, even biting his hair. "You've exchanged me!" she cried from time to time, "See, now you've exchanged me!"  Suddenly, her knee slipped, and with a little shriek, she almost fell onto the carpet. K. embraced her to keep her from falling, and was pulled down to her. "Now you belong to me," she said.
source_text: »Mag sie also jetzt Ihre Geliebte sein«, sagte Leni, »Sie würden sie aber nicht sehr vermissen, wenn Sie sie verlören oder für jemand anderen, zum Beispiel für mich, eintauschten.« »Gewiß«, sagte K. lächelnd, »das wäre denkbar, aber sie hat einen großen Vorteil Ihnen gegen über, sie weiß nichts von meinem Prozeß, und selbst wenn sie etwas davon wüßte, würde sie nicht daran denken. Sie würde mich nicht zur Nachgiebigkeit zu überreden suchen.« »Das ist kein Vorteil«, sagte Leni. »Wenn sie keine sonstigen Vorteile hat, verliere ich nicht den Mut. K. sah fast bestürzt zu ihr auf, jetzt, da sie ihm so nahe war, ging ein bitterer, aufreizender Geruch wie von Pfeffer von ihr aus, sie nahm seinen Kopf an sich, beugte sich über ihn hinweg und biß und küßte seinen Hals, biß selbst in seine Haare. »Sie haben mich eingetauscht!« rief sie von Zeit zu Zeit, »sehen Sie, nun haben Sie mich eingetauscht!« Da glitt ihr Knie aus, mit einem kleinen Schrei fiel sie fast auf den Teppich, K. umfaßte sie, um sie noch zu halten, und wurde zu ihr hinabgezogen. »Jetzt gehörst du mir«, sagte sie.
