human_translations.translator_1: Three years went by swiftly, and the Patriarch again mounted his throne to lecture to the multitude. He discussed the scholastic deliberations and parables, and he discoursed on the integument of external conduct. Suddenly he asked, “Where’s Wukong?” Wukong drew near and knelt down. “Your pupil’s here,” he said. “What sort of art have you been practicing lately?” the Patriarch asked. “Recently,” Wukong said, “your pupil has begun to apprehend the nature of all things and my foundational knowledge has become firmly established.” “If you have penetrated to the dharma nature to apprehend the origin,” said the Patriarch, “you have, in fact, entered into the divine substance. You need, however, to guard against the danger of three calamities.” When Wukong heard this, he thought for a long time and said, “The words of the master must be erroneous. I have frequently heard that when one is learned in the Way and excels in virtue, he will enjoy the same age as Heaven; fire and water cannot harm him and every kind of disease will vanish. How can there be this danger of three calamities?” “What you have learned,” said the Patriarch, “is no ordinary magic: you have stolen the creative powers of Heaven and Earth and invaded the dark mysteries of the sun and moon. Your success in perfecting the elixir is something that the gods and the demons cannot countenance. Though your appearance will be preserved and your age lengthened, after five hundred years Heaven will send down the calamity of thunder to strike you. Hence you must be intelligent and wise enough to avoid it ahead of time. If you can escape it, your age will indeed equal that of Heaven; if not, your life will thus be finished. After another five hundred years Heaven will send down the calamity of fire to burn you. That fire is neither natural nor common fire; its name is the Fire of Yin, and it arises from within the soles of your feet to reach even the cavity of your heart, reducing your entrails to ashes and your limbs to utter ruin. The arduous labor of a millennium will then have been made completely superfluous. After another five hundred years the calamity of wind will be sent to blow at you. It is not the wind from the north, south, east, or west; nor is it one of the winds of four seasons; nor is it the wind of flowers, willows, pines, and bamboos. It is called the Mighty Wind, and it enters from the top of the skull into the body, passes through the midriff, and penetrates the nine apertures.12 The bones and the flesh will be dissolved and the body itself will disintegrate. You must therefore avoid all three calamities.” When Wukong heard this, his hairs stood on end, and, kowtowing reverently, he said, “I beg the master to be merciful and impart to me the method to avoid the three calamities. To the very end, I shall never forget your gracious favor.” The Patriarch said, “It is not, in fact, difficult, except that I cannot teach you because you are somewhat different from other people.” “I have a round head pointing to Heaven,” said Wukong, “and square feet walking on Earth. Similarly, I have nine apertures and four limbs, entrails and cavities. In what way am I different from other people?” The Patriarch said, “Though you resemble a man, you have much less jowl.” The monkey, you see, has an angular face with hollow cheeks and a pointed mouth. Stretching his hand to feel himself, Wukong laughed and said, “The master does not know how to balance matters! Though I have much less jowl than human beings, I have my pouch, which may certainly be considered a compensation.” “Very well, then,” said the Patriarch, “what method of escape would you like to learn? There is the Art of the Heavenly Ladle, which numbers thirty-six transformations, and there is the Art of the Earthly Multitude, which numbers seventy-two transformations.” Wukong said, “Your pupil is always eager to catch more fishes, so I’ll learn the Art of the Earthly Multitude.” “In that case,” said the Patriarch, “come up here, and I’ll pass on the oral formulas to you.” He then whispered something into his ear, though we do not know what sort of wondrous secrets he spoke of. But this Monkey King was someone who, knowing one thing, could understand a hundred! He immediately learned the oral formulas and, after working at them and practicing them himself, he mastered all seventy-two transformations.
human_translations.translator_2: The Seeker of Secrets, having learnt the three secrets of Immortality: mind and spirit and abstinence from sex, memorized these carefully, and went on studying alone for three years more. Then the Master again mounted the platform and preached on the Parable of the Great Judgment. Suddenly he asked, “Where is the Seeker of Secrets?” The Monkey King came forward, knelt and said, “I am here.” The Master asked, “What have you been learning all this time?” “Your disciple has mastered the study of the spiritual nature.” The Master said, “Then you know the origin of things. But you must be careful of three great dangers.” The Seeker of Secrets, after pondering over this for a long time said, “I have constantly heard it said that when one has found Truth and Virtue, then one becomes an Immortal and no sickness can befall him; how then do you speak of dangers to be avoided?” The Master said, “What I teach you is not an ordinary doctrine, for it controls the forces of Heaven and Earth and the secrets of the sun, moon, and stars. When one has arrived at this stage, then one is superior to the evil spirits and the ordinary gods. Still after a time there will come a thunderclap to try your soul and spirit. If unmoved and unshaken in the deluge, you will be like Heaven itself. If you doubt, then you perish. After a long practice of religion again, one is tried a second time. This danger does not come from Heaven, nor from man, but from one’s own passions. It burns one’s whole body to ashes, and all one’s long years of practice are in vain like a dream. After another long term of practice, one is tried a third time by the danger of environment, which blows on one like a typhoon and affects one’s whole being. This must be overcome.” When the Seeker of Secrets heard this his body shook and his hair stood on end. “Oh Master, have pity on me, and tell me how to overcome these three dangers, and I shall never forget your kindness.” The Master said, “That is not difficult. There are two ways to avoid them. One has 36 wonders, the other 72; which do you wish to know?” The Seeker of Secrets said, “I wish to know the 72 wonders.” “Come here then, and I will teach you the incantation.” Then he whispered it in his ear. The Monkey King felt influences going through every pore of his body, and began to practice the arts and to learn the whole 72 wonders.
human_translations.translator_3: Another three years passed before Subodhi reappeared to teach his disciples. He spoke of academic debates and parables and of external self-cultivation. “Where’s Monkey?” he suddenly asked. Monkey kneeled before him. “Here I am!” “What have you been working on of late?” “The basics of immortality: the nature and origins of all things.” “In that case, you have already penetrated the divine substance of matter. But beware of the peril of the three calamities.” Monkey mulled this over for a while. “Master is surely mistaken,” he eventually responded. “I thought that anyone who has learned the Way and is rich in virtue will live as long as Heaven itself. Neither fire, nor water, nor illness can harm him. What three calamities do you speak of?” “What you have learned is not ordinary magic. You have stolen the creative power of heaven and earth itself, and penetrated the dark formulae of the sun and the moon. Ghosts and spirits will seek to bring you down. Although you have extended your life, in five hundred years’ time Heaven will unleash the calamity of thunder at you. You must seek wisdom to prevent this peril. Succeed and you will live as long as Heaven itself. Fail and you will die. In another five hundred years, Heaven will rain the calamity of the cold, dark fire of yin. It burns from the soles of your feet to the cavity of your heart. It will reduce your entrails to ashes and your limbs to ruins. Your millennium of hard work will then be as dust and nothingness. After another five hundred years, Heaven will set the calamity of wind onto you. This is no earthly wind. It enters through the fontanels, blows through the six internal organs, midriff, and nine orifices. Your flesh and bones will dissolve and your body will disintegrate. You see, then, why I recommend avoiding these calamities.” Monkey’s fur stood on end. “Tell me how to escape these horrors!” “Normally, this would be perfectly simple. But as you are an unusual specimen, I fear I cannot teach you.” “I’ve a head at the top and feet at the bottom, nine apertures, four limbs, five viscera, and six internal organs. How am I unusual?” “You bear a superficial resemblance to humans, but your cheeks are abnormally flat.” (Monkeys have rather angular faces, with sunken cheeks and pointed muzzles.) Monkey patted his face combatively. “Appearances can be deceptive. My cheek pouches have storage capacity on the inside. I demand parity.” “Fair enough,” considered Subodhi. “Which escape do you want to learn? There’s the Art of the Big Dipper, which involves thirty-six transformations, or the Art of the Earthly Multitude, which involves seventy-two.” “The more the merrier,” considered Monkey. “I’ll take the second.” “Come over here, then, and I will tell you the formula.” No one knows what Subodhi whispered into Monkey’s ear. But our hero was someone who could learn a hundred things from a single explanation. He immediately memorized the magic and, after practicing on his own, mastered the seventy-two transformations.
human_translations.translator_4: After three years had passed in this way the Patriarch once more sat on his lecturing throne and expounded the Dharma to the students. He recounted famous sayings and parables, and discussed external phenomena and external appearances. Without warning he asked, “Where is Sun Wukong?” Sun Wukong went forward, knelt down and replied, “Your disciple is present.” “What Way have you cultivated since coming here?” “Your disciple is now fairly well conversant with the Dharma,” Sun Wukong replied, “and my Source is getting gradually stronger.” “If you are conversant with the Dharma and you know about the Source,” the Patriarch replied, “and if the spirit has already flowed into you, then you must beware of the 'Three Disasters.'” Sun Wukong thought for a long time, then he said, “Patriarch, you're talking rubbish. I have often heard that the Way is lofty and its power mighty, that it is as eternal as Heaven, that it can overcome fire and water, and prevent all illnesses from arising, so how could there be “Three Disasters?'” To this the Patriarch replied, “This is not the ordinary Way: it involves seizing the very creation of Heaven and Earth, and encroaching on the hidden workings of the sun and moon. Once the elixir is made, devils and spirits cannot tolerate it. Although it will preserve the youthfulness of your face and prolong your life, in five hundred years' time Heaven will strike you with a thunderbolt. You must be clear-sighted in nature and mind, so that you can hide from it before it comes. If you succeed in avoiding it you will live as long as Heaven; and if you don't, it will kill you. Another five hundred years later Heaven will burn you with fire. This fire will be not heavenly fire or ordinary fire but 'hidden fire'. It will burn you from the soles of your feet to the crown of your head; your five viscera will be reduced to ashes, your four limbs will be destroyed, and a thousand years of asceticism will have been so much wasted time. Yet another five hundred years later a wind will blow at you. It will not be the North, South, East, or West wind, nor will it be a warm, fragrant wind from the Northwest; nor will it be the kind of wind that blows among flowers, willows, pine, and bamboo. It will be what is called a 'monster wind'. It will blow through the crown of your head down into your six entrails. It will go through the Cinnabar Field below your navel and penetrate your nine orifices. Your flesh and your bones will be destroyed and your body will disintegrate. So you must avoid all three of these disasters.” When he heard this Sun Wukong's hair stood on end, and he kowtowed with the words, “I implore you, my lord, to show pity and teach me how to avoid these three disasters. If you do I will be grateful to you for ever.” “That would be easy,” the Patriarch replied, “but for the fact that you are different from other people—which means that I can't.” “I have a head that faces the sky and feet standing on earth,” said Sun Wukong. “I have nine orifices and four limbs, five viscera and six entrails. How am I different from anyone else?” “Although you are quite like other people, your cheeks are too small.” Now the Monkey had a funny face, with cheeks that caved inwards and a sharp chin. Sun Wukong felt it with his hand and replied with a laugh, “Master, you didn't take everything into account. Although I'm a bit short of jaw, I've got more dewlap than other people to make up for it.” “Very well then,” the Patriarch said, “which would you prefer to learn: the thirty-six heavenly transformations or the seventy-two earthly ones?” “Your disciple wants to get as much out of it as he can, so I would like to learn the seventy-two earthly ones.” “If that's what you want,” the Patriarch replied, “come here and I'll teach you the spells.” Thereupon he whispered into Sun Wukong's ear, and who knows what miraculous spells he taught him? The Monkey King was the sort of person who understands everything once he is told a tiny part, and he learned the spells on the spot. He practiced and trained until he had mastered all seventy-two transformations.

translation: Three years had passed, and the Master once again ascended the Precious Seat, discoursing with the assembly. He spoke of case studies and illustrations, discussing external appearances and inner realities. Suddenly, he asked, “Where is Sun Wukong?” Sun Wukong stepped forward and knelt, “Disciple is here.” The Master said, “What path have you been cultivating all this while?” Sun Wukong replied, “Disciple’s nature-mind is now quite clear, and his foundation has become increasingly solid.” The Master said, “Since you have grasped the nature-mind and attained the root, you have already established the true body, yet you are merely guarding against the ‘three disasters’?” Sun Wukong, upon hearing this, pondered for a long time before saying, “Master’s words are mistaken. I have often heard that those of high virtue and enlightenment live long lives, their longevity equaling the heavens, effortlessly passing through fire and water, immune to a hundred diseases, so how can there be these ‘three disasters’?” The Master said, “This is an extraordinary path: stealing the transformations of Heaven and Earth, encroaching on the profound mysteries of the sun and moon. After the elixir is formed, spirits and deities will find it difficult to abide. Although it prolongs your years, after five hundred years, heavenly lightning will strike you. You must see your true nature, understand your mind, and preemptively avoid it. If you evade it, your life will be as long as heaven’s, but if you fail, you will perish. In another five hundred years, a fire disaster will descend. This fire is not heavenly fire, nor mortal fire, it is called ‘Yin Fire’. It erupts from the wellspring below your body, penetrating the walls of your palace, reducing your five viscera to ash and your four limbs to decay, rendering a thousand years of ascetic practice illusory. In another five hundred years, a wind disaster will arrive. This wind is not the winds of the east, west, south, or north, nor is it the winds of scorching sun or gentle breezes, it is called ‘Bie Wind’. It blows in from the top of your skull, passing through your six internal organs, the dantian, and the nine orifices, dissolving your flesh and bones, causing your body to disintegrate. That is why you must avoid them all.” Sun Wukong, upon hearing this, shivered with fear and bowed deeply, saying, “Grand Master, thank you for your merciful transmission of the method to evade the three disasters, this disciple will never forget your grace.” The Master said, “This is not difficult, but because you are different from others, I cannot pass it on to you.” Sun Wukong said, “I too have a round head that reaches the sky, feet that cover the ground, and the same nine orifices, four limbs, five viscera, and six bowels, how can I be different from others?” The Master said, “Although you resemble humans, you lack a certain something.” As it turned out, the monkey’s face was sunken, his face narrow with a pointed chin. Sun Wukong reached out to touch it and laughed, “Master, you are wrong! Though I lack a cheek, I have this pouch, which can also be folded to serve the purpose.” The Master said, “Very well, you want to learn like the others? There are thirty-six transformations of the celestial arrays, and seventy-two transformations of terrestrial perils.” Sun Wukong said, “Disciple wishes to learn one of the seventy-two terrestrial transformations.” The Master said, “Very good, come closer, and I will pass on the incantation.” He then leaned in and whispered some secret teachings. This monkey king was naturally intelligent, and once he understood a single point, all became clear. He immediately practiced and cultivated, mastering all seventy-two transformations.

human_translations.translator_3: Another three years passed before Subodhi reappeared to teach his disciples. You have stolen the creative power of heaven and earth itself, and penetrated the dark formulae of the sun and the moon. Ghosts and spirits will seek to bring you down. Although you have extended your life, in five hundred years’ time Heaven will unleash the calamity of thunder at you. You must seek wisdom to prevent this peril. Succeed and you will live as long as Heaven itself. Fail and you will die. In another five hundred years, Heaven will rain the calamity of the cold, dark fire of yin. It burns from the soles of your feet to the cavity of your heart. It will reduce your entrails to ashes and your limbs to ruins. Your millennium of hard work will then be as dust and nothingness. After another five hundred years, Heaven will set the calamity of wind onto you. This is no earthly wind. It enters through the fontanels, blows through the six internal organs, midriff, and nine orifices. Your flesh and bones will dissolve and your body will disintegrate. You see, then, why I recommend avoiding these calamities.” Monkey’s fur stood on end. “Tell me how to escape these horrors!” “Normally, this would be perfectly simple. But as you are an unusual specimen, I fear I cannot teach you.” “I’ve a head at the top and feet at the bottom, nine apertures, four limbs, five viscera, and six internal organs. How am I unusual?” “You bear a superficial resemblance to humans, but your cheeks are abnormally flat.” (Monkeys have rather angular faces, with sunken cheeks and pointed muzzles.) I demand parity.” “Fair enough,” considered Subodhi. “Which escape do you want to learn? There’s the Art of the Big Dipper, which involves thirty-six transformations, or the Art of the Earthly Multitude, which involves seventy-two.” “The more the merrier,” considered Monkey. “I’ll take the second.” “Come over here, then, and I will tell you the formula.” No one knows what Subodhi whispered into Monkey’s ear. human_translations.translator_4: After three years had passed in this way the Patriarch once more sat on his lecturing throne and expounded the Dharma to the students. He recounted famous sayings and parables, and discussed external phenomena and external appearances. Without warning he asked, “Where is Sun Wukong?” Sun Wukong went forward, knelt down and replied, “Your disciple is present.” “What Way have you cultivated since coming here?” “Your disciple is now fairly well conversant with the Dharma,” Sun Wukong replied, “and my Source is getting gradually stronger.” “If you are conversant with the Dharma and you know about the Source,” the Patriarch replied, “and if the spirit has already flowed into you, then you must beware of the 'Three Disasters.'” Sun Wukong thought for a long time, then he said, “Patriarch, you're talking rubbish. I have often heard that the Way is lofty and its power mighty, that it is as eternal as Heaven, that it can overcome fire and water, and prevent all illnesses from arising, so how could there be “Three Disasters?'” To this the Patriarch replied, “This is not the ordinary Way: it involves seizing the very creation of Heaven and Earth, and encroaching on the hidden workings of the sun and moon. Once the elixir is made, devils and spirits cannot tolerate it. Although it will preserve the youthfulness of your face and prolong your life, in five hundred years' time Heaven will strike you with a thunderbolt. You must be clear-sighted in nature and mind, so that you can hide from it before it comes. If you succeed in avoiding it you will live as long as Heaven; and if you don't, it will kill you. Another five hundred years later Heaven will burn you with fire. This fire will be not heavenly fire or ordinary fire but 'hidden fire'. It will burn you from the soles of your feet to the crown of your head; your five viscera will be reduced to ashes, your four limbs will be destroyed, and a thousand years of asceticism will have been so much wasted time. Yet another five hundred years later a wind will blow at you. It will not be the North, South, East, or West wind, nor will it be a warm, fragrant wind from the Northwest; nor will it be the kind of wind that blows among flowers, willows, pine, and bamboo. It will be what is called a 'monster wind'. It will blow through the crown of your head down into your six entrails. It will go through the Cinnabar Field below your navel and penetrate your nine orifices. Your flesh and your bones will be destroyed and your body will disintegrate. So you must avoid all three of these disasters.” When he heard this Sun Wukong's hair stood on end, and he kowtowed with the words, “I implore you, my lord, to show pity and teach me how to avoid these three disasters. If you do I will be grateful to you for ever.” “That would be easy,” the Patriarch replied, “but for the fact that you are different from other people—which means that I can't.” “I have a head that faces the sky and feet standing on earth,” said Sun Wukong. “I have nine orifices and four limbs, five viscera and six entrails. How am I different from anyone else?” “Although you are quite like other people, your cheeks are too small.” Now the Monkey had a funny face, with cheeks that caved inwards and a sharp chin. Sun Wukong felt it with his hand and replied with a laugh, “Master, you didn't take everything into account. Although I'm a bit short of jaw, I've got more dewlap than other people to make up for it.” “Very well then,” the Patriarch said, “which would you prefer to learn: the thirty-six heavenly transformations or the seventy-two earthly ones?” “Your disciple wants to get as much out of it as he can, so I would like to learn the seventy-two earthly ones.” “If that's what you want,” the Patriarch replied, “come here and I'll teach you the spells.” Thereupon he whispered into Sun Wukong's ear, and who knows what miraculous spells he taught him? The Monkey King was the sort of person who understands everything once he is told a tiny part, and he learned the spells on the spot. He practiced and trained until he had mastered all seventy-two transformations.

translation:
Three years had passed. The Master ascended the throne once more and spoke to the gathered crowd. He discussed koans and parables, expounding on outward appearances and inner substance. Suddenly, he asked, "Where is Sun Wukong?" Sun Wukong stepped forward and knelt. "Disciple is here." The Master said, "What path have you been cultivating?" Sun Wukong replied, "Disciple's Dharma nature has become quite clear, and my root is growing increasingly solid." The Master said, "Since you have grasped Dharma nature and rooted yourself, you've already cultivated your shen body, yet you only focus on avoiding the 'three calamities.'" Sun Wukong, upon hearing this, pondered deeply and said, "Master, your words are mistaken. I've often heard that those of high virtue live long, equaling Heaven's lifespan, crossing fire and water unharmed, free from a hundred illnesses, so how can there be these three calamities?" The Master said, "This is the extraordinary way: it steals Heaven and Earth's transformations, violates the mysteries of the sun and moon; after the elixir is formed, spirits and demons cannot bear it. Although it prolongs one's appearance, after five hundred years, a heavenly thunderbolt will strike you, and you must realize your true nature and open your mind to avoid it. If you evade it, you will live as long as Heaven; if you cannot, your life will end. Another five hundred years later, a heavenly fire will descend upon you. This fire is not heavenly fire nor mortal fire; it is called 'yin fire.' It rises from the wellspring beneath your body, burning through your earthen palace, turning your five organs to ash and your limbs to decay, rendering your thousand years of ascetic practice illusory. Another five hundred years, and a wind calamity will blow upon you. This wind is not the southeast wind, northwest wind, wind of incense, moon, gold, nor the wind of flowers, willows, pine, or bamboo; it is called 'bi wind.' It blows from the fontanelle, enters your six organs, passes through the dantian, pierces the nine orifices, causing your bones and flesh to become loose, and your body to dissolve. Thus, you must all avoid these calamities."

Sun Wukong, upon hearing this, felt his hair stand on end and bowed his head in reverence, saying, "Master, your immense grace, passing down the methods to avoid the three calamities, I shall never forget your kindness." The Master said, "This is not difficult, it's just that you are different from others, so I cannot pass it on directly." Sun Wukong said, "I have a round head, stand on two feet, possess nine orifices and four limbs, five organs and six internal organs. How am I different from others?" The Master said, "Although you resemble a human, you lack cheeks." It turned out that the monkey had a narrow face, sunken cheeks, and a pointed mouth. Sun Wukong stretched out his hand and touched his face, laughing and saying, "Master, you've made a mistake! Although I lack cheeks, I have this pouch of fur, which can also be used to avoid them." The Master said, "Very well, if you wish to learn like an ordinary person, you need to understand the celestial and terrestrial transformations. There are thirty-six celestial transformations and seventy-two terrestrial transformations." Sun Wukong said, "Disciple wishes to learn one terrestrial transformation." The Master said, "Very well, come forward and I will teach you the mantra." He leaned in close and whispered something incomprehensible. This monkey king was quick to understand, and once he grasped the mantra, he practiced and refined it himself, mastering all seventy-two terrestrial transformations.

You have stolen the creative power of heaven and earth itself, and penetrated the dark formulae of the sun and the moon. Ghosts and spirits will seek to bring you down. Although you have extended your life, in five hundred years’ time Heaven will unleash the calamity of thunder at you. You must seek wisdom to prevent this peril. Succeed and you will live as long as Heaven itself. Fail and you will die. In another five hundred years, Heaven will rain the calamity of the cold, dark fire of yin. It burns from the soles of your feet to the cavity of your heart. It will reduce your entrails to ashes and your limbs to ruins. Your millennium of hard work will then be as dust and nothingness. After another five hundred years, Heaven will set the calamity of wind onto you. This is no earthly wind. It enters through the fontanels, blows through the six internal organs, midriff, and nine orifices. Your flesh and bones will dissolve and your body will disintegrate. You see, then, why I recommend avoiding these calamities.” Monkey’s fur stood on end. “Tell me how to escape these horrors!” “Normally, this would be perfectly simple. But as you are an unusual specimen, I fear I cannot teach you.” “I’ve a head at the top and feet at the bottom, nine apertures, four limbs, five viscera, and six internal organs. How am I unusual?” “You bear a superficial resemblance to humans, but your cheeks are abnormally flat.” (Monkeys have rather angular faces, with sunken cheeks and pointed muzzles.) Monkey patted his face combatively. “Appearances can be deceptive. My cheek pouches have storage capacity on the inside. I demand parity.” “Fair enough,” considered Subodhi. “Which escape do you want to learn? There’s the Art of the Big Dipper, which involves thirty-six transformations, or the Art of the Earthly Multitude, which involves seventy-two.” “The more the merrier,” considered Monkey. “I’ll take the second.” “Come over here, then, and I will tell you the formula.” No one knows what Subodhi whispered into Monkey’s ear. But our hero was someone who could learn a hundred things from a single explanation. He immediately memorized the magic and, after practicing on his own, mastered the seventy-two transformations.
human_translations.translator_4: After three years had passed in this way the Patriarch once more sat on his lecturing throne and expounded the Dharma to the students. He recounted famous sayings and parables, and discussed external phenomena and external appearances. Without warning he asked, “Where is Sun Wukong?” Sun Wukong went forward, knelt down and replied, “Your disciple is present.” “What Way have you cultivated since coming here?” “Your disciple is now fairly well conversant with the Dharma,” Sun Wukong replied, “and my Source is getting gradually stronger.” “If you are conversant with the Dharma and you know about the Source,” the Patriarch replied, “and if the spirit has already flowed into you, then you must beware of the 'Three Disasters.'” Sun Wukong thought for a long time, then he said, “Patriarch, you're talking rubbish. I have often heard that the Way is lofty and its power mighty, that it is as eternal as Heaven, that it can overcome fire and water, and prevent all illnesses from arising, so how could there be “Three Disasters?'” To this the Patriarch replied, “This is not the ordinary Way: it involves seizing the very creation of Heaven and Earth, and encroaching on the hidden workings of the sun and moon. Once the elixir is made, devils and spirits cannot tolerate it. Although it will preserve the youthfulness of your face and prolong your life, in five hundred years' time Heaven will strike you with a thunderbolt. You must be clear-sighted in nature and mind, so that you can hide from it before it comes. If you succeed in avoiding it you will live as long as Heaven; and if you don't, it will kill you. Another five hundred years later Heaven will burn you with fire. This fire will be not heavenly fire or ordinary fire but 'hidden fire'. It will burn you from the soles of your feet to the crown of your head; your five viscera will be reduced to ashes, your four limbs will be destroyed, and a thousand years of asceticism will have been so much wasted time. Yet another five hundred years later a wind will blow at you. It will not be the North, South, East, or West wind, nor will it be a warm, fragrant wind from the Northwest; nor will it be the kind of wind that blows among flowers, willows, pine, and bamboo. It will be what is called a 'monster wind'. It will blow through the crown of your head down into your six entrails. It will go through the Cinnabar Field below your navel and penetrate your nine orifices. Your flesh and your bones will be destroyed and your body will disintegrate. So you must avoid all three of these disasters.” When he heard this Sun Wukong's hair stood on end, and he kowtowed with the words, “I implore you, my lord, to show pity and teach me how to avoid these three disasters. If you do I will be grateful to you for ever.” “That would be easy,” the Patriarch replied, “but for the fact that you are different from other people—which means that I can't.” “I have a head that faces the sky and feet standing on earth,” said Sun Wukong. “I have nine orifices and four limbs, five viscera and six entrails. How am I different from anyone else?” “Although you are quite like other people, your cheeks are too small.” Now the Monkey had a funny face, with cheeks that caved inwards and a sharp chin. Sun Wukong felt it with his hand and replied with a laugh, “Master, you didn't take everything into account. Although I'm a bit short of jaw, I've got more dewlap than other people to make up for it.” “Very well then,” the Patriarch said, “which would you prefer to learn: the thirty-six heavenly transformations or the seventy-two earthly ones?” “Your disciple wants to get as much out of it as he can, so I would like to learn the seventy-two earthly ones.” “If that's what you want,” the Patriarch replied, “come here and I'll teach you the spells.” Thereupon he whispered into Sun Wukong's ear, and who knows what miraculous spells he taught him? The Monkey King was the sort of person who understands everything once he is told a tiny part, and he learned the spells on the spot. He practiced and trained until he had mastered all seventy-two transformations.

translation: "Having won this battle, let me dispatch someone to fetch the Mahayana sutras, then, with pure sincerity, I will resume the practice of good fruits." All the officials obeyed. At that time, someone in the temple asked: "Who is willing to carry out my imperial decree and journey to the West to prostrate oneself before the Buddha and seek the sutras?" No one answered. At that moment, a monk stepped forward, bowing before the emperor, and said: "This poor monk is unworthy, but I wish to serve with the devotion of a dog or horse, and accompany Your Majesty to seek the true sutras, praying for the eternal stability of our kingdom." The Tang emperor was overjoyed and stepped forward, taking the monk's hand, saying: "If you truly possess such loyalty and wisdom, and are not afraid of the long journey and the arduous journey across mountains and rivers, I am willing to acknowledge you as my brother." Xuanzang bowed his head in gratitude. The Tang emperor was indeed a very virtuous man. He went to the temple before Buddha and, with Xuanzang, performed four prostrations, calling him "my imperial brother, the holy monk." Xuanzang thanked him profusely, saying: "Your Majesty, what merit or ability do I have to deserve such heavenly grace? I shall devote myself wholeheartedly and journey to the West without fail. If I fail to reach the West and obtain the true sutras, I will not return even if it means death, and I shall forever fall into the hells." He then picked up incense and offered it before Buddha, making a vow. The Tang emperor was very pleased. He immediately ordered the court to return, awaiting a favorable day and auspicious hour to issue a dispatch for his departure, and thus the court dispersed.
source_text: “且收胜会，待我差人取得大乘经来，再秉丹诚，重修善果。”众官无不遵依。当时在寺中问曰：“谁肯领朕旨意，上西天拜佛求经？”问不了，旁边闪过法师，帝前施礼道：“贫僧不才，愿效犬马之劳，与陛下求取真经，祈保我王江山永固。”唐王大喜，上前将御手扶起道：“法师果能尽此忠贤，不怕程途遥远，跋涉山川，朕情愿与你拜为兄弟。”玄奘顿首谢恩。唐王果是十分贤德，就去那寺里佛前，与玄奘拜了四拜，口称“御弟圣僧”。玄奘感谢不尽道：“陛下，贫僧有何德何能，敢蒙天恩眷顾如此？我这一去，定要捐躯努力，直至西天。如不到西天，不得真经，即死也不敢回国，永堕沉沦地狱。”随在佛前拈香，以此为誓。唐王甚喜，即命回銮，待选良利日辰，发牒出行，遂此驾回各散。
gt_translation: "Let's end the victory meeting, wait until I send someone to obtain the Mahayana Sutra, and then I will be honest and re-cultivate the good fruits." All the officials obeyed. At that time, I asked in the temple, "Who is willing to follow my will and go to the west to worship Buddha and seek scriptures?" I couldn't ask, but a Dharma master flashed by, and the emperor saluted and said: "The poor monk is not talented, I would like to do the hard work of dogs and horses, and seek truth with Your Majesty. The scriptures, pray to keep my king Jiangshan forever." Tang Wang was overjoyed, and he stepped forward and lifted his hand up and said: "The Master can do this loyal and virtuous, not afraid of the long journey, trekking mountains and rivers, I would rather worship you as a brother." Xuan Zang thanked him. Tang Wangguo was very virtuous, so he went to the temple in front of the Buddha, and worshipped Xuanzang four times, and he was called "the royal brother and holy monk". Xuanzang thanked him endlessly and said, "Your Majesty, what kind of virtue and ability does a poor monk have, and dare to be favored by the heavens like this? When I go, I must sacrifice my life and work hard until I reach the Western Heaven. If you dare to go back to your country, you will fall into hell forever." He sipped incense in front of the Buddha, taking this as an oath. Tang Wang was very happy, so he ordered him to return to Luang, waiting for a good day to be selected, and issued an ultimatum to go out, so he drove back to the various places.

human_translations.translator_1: We shall then renew our sincere effort to cultivate the fruits of virtue.” Not one of the officials disagreed with the emperor, who then asked in the temple, “Who is willing to accept our commission to seek scriptures from Buddha in the Western Heaven?” Hardly had he finished speaking when the Master of the Law stepped from the side and saluted him, saying, “Though your poor monk has no talents, he is ready to perform the service of a dog and a horse. I shall seek these true scriptures on behalf of Your Majesty, that the empire of our king may be firm and everlasting.” Highly pleased, the Tang emperor went forward to raise up the monk with his royal hands, saying, “If the Master is willing to express his loyalty this way, undaunted by the great distance or by the journey over mountains and streams, we are willing to become bond brothers with you.” Xuanzang touched his forehead to the ground to express his gratitude. Being indeed a righteous man, the Tang emperor went at once before Buddha’s image in the temple and bowed to Xuanzang four times, addressing him as “our brother and holy monk.” Deeply moved, Xuanzang said, “Your Majesty, what ability and what virtue does your poor monk possess that he should merit such affection from your Heavenly Grace? I shall not spare myself in this journey, but I shall proceed with all diligence until I reach the Western Heaven. If I do not attain my goal, or the true scriptures, I shall not return to our land even if I have to die. I would rather fall into eternal perdition in Hell.” He thereupon lifted the incense before Buddha and made that his vow. Highly pleased, the Tang emperor ordered his carriage back to the palace to wait for the auspicious day and hour, when official documents could be issued for the journey to begin. And so the Throne withdrew as everyone dispersed.
human_translations.translator_2: The pilgrim was to be accompanied by his chief disciple, the Sun the Seeker of Emptiness, Zhu the Seeker of Strength, and Sha the Seeker of Purity. And so on and so on. On hearing this Sha the Monk could not wait any longer, but cried out, “Brother Sun, the Master has lost his felt bag and the emperor’s edict, and now I see you have them. Do not heed the Master’s behavior towards you. Come back and let us continue our journey for the Sacred Scriptures. But if you are unwilling to return, I beg of you a thousand times to let me have the bag with the emperor’s edict.” The false Sun laughed coldly and said, “Having read this edict, I will myself go to the West for the Sacred Scriptures and acquire merit and make a name for myself that shall never be forgotten.” Sha the Monk replied, “That is impossible! It was never said that a monkey was to procure the Scriptures. If the Master does not go with you, Buddha will not give you the Scriptures.” The impostor answered, “But I have provided myself with a duplicate Master.”
human_translations.translator_3: “Deepest thanks.” Tripitaka bowed to him. Boqin returned the bow and they went their separate ways. Tripitaka and his new, still naked disciple set off across the Mountain of Two Frontiers. Soon enough, yet another tiger presented itself, snarling and swishing its tail. Tripitaka—on horseback—cowered; Monkey, by contrast, was delighted: “ Don’t worry, Master. He’s just here to deliver some clothes.” He pulled the needle-shaped iron out of his ear: with one wave, it became a thick cudgel. “Time to give my precious a little exercise, after five hundred years’ rest.” He strode up to the tiger. “Where do you think you’re going?” While the tiger crouched, as if mesmerized, Monkey with one blow smashed its brains and teeth into a gory porridge. Tripitaka rolled off his horse in terror at Monkey’s deadly speed.
human_translations.translator_4: If anyone is willing to go for them, His reward will be a golden body.” When he had read these lines Taizong issued an order to the assembly of monks: “Suspend this service until we have sent someone to fetch the scriptures of the Great Vehicle, and then you shall once more strive sincerely to achieve good retribution.” The monks all obeyed his instructions. The Emperor then asked those present in the monastery, “Who is willing to accept our commission to go to the Western Heaven to visit the Buddha and fetch the scriptures?” Before he had finished his question, the Master of the Law came forward, bowed low in greeting, and said, “Although I am lacking in ability, I would like to offer my humble efforts to fetch the true scriptures for Your Majesty and thus ensure the eternal security of your empire.” The Tang Emperor, who was overjoyed to hear this, went forward to raise him to his feet. “Master,” he said, “if you are prepared to exert your loyalty and wisdom to the full, not fearing the length of the journey or the rivers and mountains you will have to cross, I shall make you my own sworn brother.” Xuanzang kowtowed to thank him. As the Tang Emperor was indeed a man of wisdom and virtue he went to a place before the Buddha in the monastery where he bowed to Xuanzang four times, calling him “younger brother” and “holy monk.” Xuanzang thanked him effusively. “Your Majesty,” he said, “I have no virtue or talent that fits me for the sacred honour of being treated as your kinsman. On this journey I shall give my all and go straight to the Western Heaven. If I fail to reach there or to obtain the true scriptures, then I shall not return to this country even in death, and shall fall for eternity into Hell.” He burned incense in front of the Buddha to mark this vow. The happy Emperor ordered his chariot to take him back to the palace; later on an auspicious day would be chosen on which Xuanzang would be given a passport and set out. With that he returned and everyone dispersed.

translation:
"Let the victory feast be held. I shall dispatch someone to procure the Great Vehicle scriptures, and then, with a sincere heart, I will re-cultivate good fortune."  All the officials readily obeyed. At that time, someone in the temple inquired: "Who will take my decree and go west to pay homage to the Buddha and seek the scriptures?" No one answered. Suddenly, a monk stepped forward and bowed before the Emperor: "I am but a humble monk, willing to do the humble work of a dog or horse, and accompany Your Majesty in seeking the true scriptures, praying for the perpetuity of our kingdom." The Tang Emperor was overjoyed and rose to support him, saying, "You are indeed a loyal and virtuous minister. Fear not the long journey and the arduous paths. I am willing to make you my sworn brother." Xuanzang bowed deeply in thanks. 

Indeed, the Tang Emperor was a wise and benevolent ruler. He went before the Buddha in the temple and, with Xuanzang, performed four bows, proclaiming, "My sworn brother, the holy monk." Xuanzang, overwhelmed with gratitude, said, "Your Majesty, what merit or capability do I possess to be so favored by Heaven? When I depart, I will certainly expend my life and effort until I reach the West Heaven. If I do not reach the West Heaven and obtain the true scriptures, even if I die, I will not dare return to the country, forever falling into the abyss of hell." He then held incense before the Buddha, taking an oath. The Tang Emperor was delighted and ordered the royal procession to return. He awaited a favorable day and auspicious hour, and issued an edict for the journey. Thus, the journey commenced, and everyone dispersed.

translation:
Singing and drinking to my heart’s content,
Let my long song and sighs follow the wind.
Calling on my brothers and friends, I invite fellow travelers,
Gathering companions and close friends in the wilds.

We play games and pass the cups,
And words fly freely like the chimes.
Shrimp and crab are cooked morning and night,
Duck and chicken are roasted daily.

The simple wife pours tea with a carefree heart,
The mountain wife cooks with composure.

At dawn I take my staff and wade through the shallows,
At sunrise, I carry firewood across the rapids.

After the rain, I don my raincoat to catch carp,
Facing the wind, I swing my axe to fell dry pine.

Hiding my tracks and blending with the world,
I take on the guise of a fool.

Zhang Shao said, “Brother Li, I have only begun a line,
Now it’s my turn, brother, I will begin a pair,
And I, too, shall continue it.”

A wild man who embraces the moon and the wind,
A hermit who finds solace in the old age of the river.

With a portion of leisure, we embrace the carefree,
Our tongues never speaking of joy or tranquility.
One sleeps soundly in a thatched hut by night,
One shelters beneath a simple reed mat when night falls.

We make friends with pine and plum trees,
And we form an alliance with birds and herons.

Calculation of gain and loss is absent from our minds,
The sounds of war are unheard.
Every day, we enjoy a cup of sweet wine,
We nourish ourselves with simple vegetables.

Two bundles of firewood provide for life,
A fishing rod is our livelihood.

I hear my children grinding their axes,
And I call my son to mend the old cloth.

When spring arrives, I love to see the willow trees turn green,
And I delight in watching the reeds and sedges turn blue.
In summer, I avoid the heat to cultivate new bamboo,
In June, I enjoy the coolness by picking young lotus.

When the frost descends, we slaughter fat chickens daily,
And on the Double Ninth Festival, we cook the plump crabs.
In winter, the sun sets while I sleep,
The day after the 9th frost, I don't cook the fish.
source_text: 自唱自斟随放荡，长歌长叹任颠风。呼兄唤弟邀船伙，挈友携朋聚野翁。行令猜拳频递盏，拆牌道字漫传钟。烹虾煮蟹朝朝乐，炒鸭爊鸡日日丰。愚妇煎茶情散诞，山妻造饭意从容。晓来举杖淘轻浪，日出担柴过大冲。雨后披蓑擒活鲤，风前弄斧伐枯松。潜踪避世妆痴蠢，隐姓埋名作哑聋。”张稍道：“李兄，我才僭先起句，今到我兄，也先起一联，小弟亦当续之。”“风月佯狂山野汉，江湖寄傲老余丁。清闲有分随潇洒，口舌无闻喜太平。月夜身眠茅屋稳，天昏体盖箬蓑轻。忘情结识松梅友，乐意相交鸥鹭盟。名利心头无算计，干戈耳畔不闻声。随时一酌香醪酒，度日三餐野菜羹。两束柴薪为活计，一竿钓线是营生。闲呼稚子磨钢斧，静唤憨儿补旧缯。春到爱观杨柳绿，时融喜看荻芦青。夏天避暑修新竹，六月乘凉摘嫩菱。霜降鸡肥常日宰，重阳蟹壮及时烹。冬来日上还沉睡，数九天高自不蒸。
gt_translation: Self-singing, self-pouring, and debauchery, long songs and long sighs, let the wind blow. Calling brothers and brothers to invite shipmates, and friends to gather together with friends. The orders to guess boxing are frequently handed over, and the words of the demolition of cards are passed on. Cooked shrimp and boiled crabs are happy, fried duck and chicken are prosperous every day. The Fool's Wife's love for sencha is scattered, and the Shan's wife makes meals calmly. Xiaolai raises his stick to scour the light waves, and the sun rises too much to carry firewood. Catch the live carp with minnows after the rain, and cut down withered pine with an axe before the wind. Hidden from the world makeup is stupid, incognito is deaf. "Zhang Shao said: "Brother Li, I just started the sentence first. Now that I come to my brother, I will also start a couplet first, and my younger brother should continue it." "" Fengyue pretends to be a wild man in the mountains, and the rivers and lakes are proud of the old Yu Ding. Leisure and dashing, with no tongue in sight, hi peace. On the moonlit night, the body sleeps in the thatched hut, and when the sky is dizzy, the body is lightly covered. Forgetting to meet Songmei friends, I am willing to meet Ou Lumeng. Fame and fortune have no plans in mind, and there is no sound in the ears of fighting. Have a sip of mashed wine at any time, and spend three meals a day with wild vegetable soup. Two bundles of firewood are for work, and a fishing line is for living. Silently calling the child to sharpen the steel axe, and quietly calling for the Han'er to mend the old one. When spring arrives, I like to see willow green, and Shi Rong likes to see dilu green. Hsinchu is cultivated in summer, and tender lings are picked in the cool of June. Shuangjiang chicken fat is slaughtered every day, and Chongyang crabs are cooked in time. In winter, the sun is still sleeping, counting nine days without steaming.

human_translations.translator_1: I sing and freely pour on my heart’s desire; In songs and sighs there’s none to restrain me. I call fellow boatmen to come as brothers; With friends we join the codgers of the wilds. We make rules, play games, and exchange the cups; We break words, remake them, when we pass the mugs. Cooked shrimps, boiled crabs are my daily feasts; I’m daily fed by smoked fowls and fried ducks. My unlettered wife makes tea languidly; My mountain wife cooks rice most leisurely. When dawn comes, I lift my staff to stir the waves; At sunrise I pole my wood to cross big roads. I don coir coat after rain to catch live carps; Wind-blown I wield my ax to cut dried pines. Hiding tracks to flee the world, I’m like a fool; Blotting name and surname, I play deaf and dumb. Zhang Shao said, “Brother Li, just now I presumed to take the lead and began with the first line of the poem. Why don’t you begin this time and I shall follow you.” A rustic who feigns to be romantic; An oldie taking pride in streams and lakes. My lot is leisure, I seek laxity and ease. Shunning talk and gossip, I love my peace. In moonlit nights I sleep in safe straw huts; When sky dims I’m draped with light coir cape. I befriend with ardor both pines and plums; I’m pleased to mingle with egrets and gulls. My mind has no plans for fortune or fame; My ears are deaf to the din of spear and drum. At any time I’d pour my fragrant wine; My day’s three meals are soups of leafy greens. My living rests on two bundles of wood; My trade is my pole fit with hooks and lines. I call our young son to sharpen my ax; I tell my small rogue he should mend our nets. Spring comes, I love to watch the willows green; Warm days gladden the sight of rushes and reeds. To flee summer’s heat I plant new bamboos; I pick young lotus to cool myself in June. When Frost Descends the fatted fowls are slain; By Double Ninth11 I’d cook the roe-filled crabs. I sleep deep in winter though the sun is high; When the sky’s tall and hazy, I’d not fry!
human_translations.translator_2: And to the tree of nature. Recognize no traitor as friend, Follow no artificial rules Lest you be deceived. Strike hard with your fist, But without malice. The apparent method is not real, The light of sun and of moon, Wherein lies their difference? Having traveled on, they came to a village where they sought lodgings, but the people were greatly frightened at the sight of Zhu Bajie with his long snout and flapping ears. So Sun advised him to hide his snout in his bosom and fasten his ears, to prevent them flapping. Food was served them, and the Master asked a blessing. Zhu Bajie ate ravenously. The host’s name was Wang and he said, “Before you there is a great mountain 800 li to cross. You should be well armed, as the mountain is full of robbers and demons.” They started West again, but had not gone far when a terrible storm arose, which blew the Master from his horse, and a tiger came rushing on him. Zhu Bajie took his nine pronged spear and said, “Come on, I will soon finish you.”
human_translations.translator_4: Singing and musing to myself I'm as wild as I care to be; Long songs, long sighs, I can let myself be crazy. I invite my brothers and cousins and fellow boatmen; Leading my friends by the hand I meet the old man of the wilds. As we play guess-fingers the cups fly fast; When we make riddles the goblets slowly circulate. Saute or boiled crab is a delight every morning; Plenty of fried duck and chicken cooked in ashes every day. As my simple wife brews tea, my spirits are untrammelled; While my mountain spouse cooks supper, my mind is at ease. At the coming of dawn I wash my stick in the ripples; When the sun rises I carry firewood across the road. After the rain I put on my cloak to catch live carp; I wield my axe before the wind to fell a withered pine. I cover my tracks and hide from the world, acting the imbecile; I change my name and pretend to be deaf and dumb. “Brother Li,” said Zhang Shao. “I unfairly took the first lines just now, so now it's your turn to compose the first lines while I follow you.” Thus they continued: The man of the mountains acting mad under wind and moon; The haughty and unwanted dotard of the river. With his share of idleness, and able to be quite free; No sound from his voice as he revels in his peace. On moonlit nights he sleeps secure in a cottage of thatch; He lightly covers himself at dusk with clothes of reed. His passion spent, he befriends the pine and the plum; He is happy to be the companion of cormorant and gull. Fame and profit count for nothing in his mind; His ears have never heard the clash of arms. One is always pouring out fresh rice-wine, The other has wild vegetable soup with every meal. One makes a living with two bundles of firewood; The other supports himself with rod and line. One idly tells his innocent son to sharpen the axe of steel; The other quietly bids his slow-witted child to mend the nets. In spring one likes to see the willows turning green; When the seasons change the other enjoys the rushes' blue. Avoiding the summer heat, one trims the new bamboo; The other gathers water-chestnuts on cool July evenings. When frost begins, plump chickens are killed each day; In mid-autumn the crabs are at their best and always in the pot. When the sun rises in winter, the one is still asleep; The other keeps cool in the dog days of summer.

translation:
Singing and pouring for my own enjoyment, I raise a long song and sigh, letting the wind carry it.

I call out to my brothers and companions, inviting them onto the boat, gathering friends and fellow travelers under the wild pavilion. 

We play games, gamble, and pass the cups, our laughter echoing through the bells.  

We cook shrimp and crab, feasting day and night. The foolish wife steeps tea with a carefree smile, the mountain wife cooks with a tranquil mind.

At dawn, I take my staff and walk light-footed through the shallows, at sunrise, I carry firewood across the rapids.

After the rain, I put on my raincoat and catch live carp, before the wind, I swing my axe to chop down dead pines.

I wander off the beaten path, pretending to be foolish and simple, concealing my name and fading into anonymity.

Zhang Shao said, “Brother Li, I just started the poem, now it’s my turn, I'll also offer a couplet, and my younger brother will continue it."

A mad man, wild with the wind and moon, a mountain man unburdened by the world. 

In leisure, I enjoy freedom, in silence, I find contentment.

I sleep soundly in my thatched hut by moonlight, I cover myself with a straw raincoat as night deepens.

I make friends with the pine and plum trees, joyously associating with birds and herons.

I care not for fame and fortune, I hear no clamor of war.

Every day I drink a cup of fragrant wine, and for three meals, I eat vegetable gruel. 

Two bundles of firewood sustain me, a fishing rod is my livelihood.

I playfully call to the children to sharpen their axes, quietly summon the boy to mend old cloth. 

When spring arrives, I enjoy watching the willows turn green, I rejoice to see the reeds and rush grow lush.

In summer, I avoid the heat by tending new bamboo shoots, in June, I gather young lotus pods for a cool respite.

When frost descends, the chickens are fattened and slaughtered daily, on the Double Ninth Festival, the crabs are ready for cooking.

When winter arrives, the sun rises late, even as the Ninth Frost approaches, I do not feel the chill.

translation:
Singing and pouring, I drink freely,
Chanting and sighing, I submit to the wind's whims.
I call my brothers and invite shipmates,
Gathering friends and companions, we become wild hermits.

We play games, pass cups, and make toasts,
Our cards spread, words fly through the clock's chime.
Cooking shrimp and crab, our days are full of joy,
Stir-frying duck and chicken, our days are plentiful.

Simple wives brew tea, their thoughts drift carefree,
Mountain wives cook with calm and ease.
At dawn, I raise my staff to skim the light waves,
At sunrise, I carry firewood across the rushing stream.

After rain, I wear my raincoat to catch live carp,
Before the wind, I swing my axe to fell dead pines.

I hide my tracks, evade the world, feigning foolishness,
I conceal my name, bury my identity, becoming deaf and dumb.

Zhang Shao said, "Li brother, I only dared to begin a verse,
Now it's my turn, brother, I'll also start a couplet,
My younger brother will continue it."

"Reckless and wild like the moon and wind,
A mountain dweller, I take refuge in the river's embrace.
Enjoyment comes in finding one's place,
Silence and tranquility, a happy life.

In the moonlit night, I sleep soundly in my thatched hut,
As dusk descends, I cover myself with a light reed mat.
In a heart free of attachments, I forge friendships with pine and plum,
Willingly, I cultivate alliances with birds and gulls.

No place for fame and wealth in my thoughts,
War drums are unheard in my ears.
Every time, a sip of fragrant rice wine,
My days pass by with three meals of wild herbs.

Two bundles of firewood are my livelihood,
One fishing pole is my means of earning a living.
Leisurely, I call to my child to sharpen the axe,
Peacefully, I call to my child to mend old cloth.

Spring arrives, I delight in the green willow,
I rejoice in seeing the green reeds and rushes.

In summer, I seek refuge from the heat, planting new bamboo,
In June, I take shelter from the heat, picking young lotus.

As frost descends, chickens are plump, slaughtered every day,
On Double Ninth Day, crabs are fat, cooked just in time.

In winter, the sun rises late and I still sleep,
On the ninth day of winter, the sky is high and I do not sweat.

translation:
He drinks and sings freely, letting out long songs and sighs to the swaying wind. He calls for his brothers and companions, gathering fellow travelers in the wild. They play dice, guess rhymes, and pass cups to one another, laughing. They eat braised prawns and boiled crabs every day, and fried ducks and roast chickens are plentiful each day. The rustic wife brews tea with a carefree heart, while the mountain wife cooks with a peaceful disposition.  He takes his staff in the morning and walks into the gentle waves. At sunrise, he carries firewood across the large rapids. After the rain, he dons his rain cloak and catches live carp. In the wind, he wields his axe to fell dead pines.

He hides his tracks, evading the world, pretending to be simple and foolish, and burying his name to live as deaf and mute.  Zhang Shao said, "Li brother, I have just started a line. Now that it's my brother's turn, I will start a couplet as well, and my younger brother will continue it." 
"A wild man in the mountains, living under the moon and wind, a solitary man content in the rivers and lakes. A carefree spirit, living freely and easily, happy in the quietude and tranquility. At night, he sleeps soundly in his thatched hut. When the sky darkens, he covers himself with a light reed mat. 

He makes friends with pine and plum blossoms, and enjoys the company of gulls and herons. He has no desire for fame and fortune, and does not hear the sounds of war. He drinks fragrant rice wine whenever he pleases, and eats vegetable soup for every meal. Two bundles of firewood are his livelihood, and a fishing rod is his trade. In his leisure, he watches his children sharpen their axes, and quietly calls to his son to mend old cloth. When spring arrives, he enjoys watching the willow trees turn green, and in summer he likes to see the reeds and rush turn blue.

In summer, he seeks shade by planting new bamboo. In June, he enjoys the coolness and picks fresh lotus seeds. When the frost comes, he slaughters the fattened chickens. During the Double Ninth Festival, he cooks the plump crabs. When winter comes, he sleeps late even when the sun rises high, and doesn't worry about the cold.

translation:
Drinking to my own tune, pouring my own cup, I let go of decorum, singing a long song, sighing deeply, surrendering to the wind. 

Calling on brothers and companions, I invite my friends to join me in the wild. We play games, hand over cups in a flurry, and stories and words fill the hours.

We cook shrimp and crab, feasting joyfully every day; we stir-fry duck and roast chicken, abundant blessings every day.

The foolish wife brews tea, her emotions freely dispersed; the mountain wife prepares the meals, her intentions serene.

In the morning, I take my staff and tap the gently rolling waves; at sunrise, I carry firewood across the rushing torrent.

After the rain, I don my raincoat and catch live carp; in the wind, I swing my axe and fell the withered pines.

Hiding my tracks, I shun the world, feigning stupidity; I conceal my name and hide my identity, acting deaf and dumb. 

Zhang Shao said: "Brother Li, I have just begun the first line, now it is my turn to continue. Younger brother, I will add another line."

"Wind and moon, madmen in the mountains, wild men of the rivers and lakes, I am the one left, old and with no occupation but contentment.

With ease, I live freely and openly; no sound of contention reaches my ears, only the joy of peace.

At night, I lie in my thatched hut, content; in the dark, I shelter beneath my raincoat, light as a feather.

I forget worldly attachments, and in friendship with pines and plum blossoms, I find joy in the companionship of gulls and herons.

Calculation of wealth and honor holds no place in my heart; the clang of weapons is unheard by my ears.

At any time, a cup of fragrant wine, three meals of wild vegetables sustain me.

Two bundles of firewood sustain my livelihood, a fishing rod is my craft.

I playfully call to the young children to sharpen their axes; I quietly summon the simple boy to mend the old cloth.

In spring, I delight in the sight of willow leaves turning green; in summer, I enjoy watching the rushes and reeds turn blue.

In summer's heat, I plant new bamboo; in June, I enjoy the coolness and pick ripe lotus seeds.

As frost descends, the chickens grow fat, ready for the slaughter; on the Double Ninth festival, I cook plump crabs.

Winter comes, the sun rises late, I sleep soundly; as the Ninth Night of winter approaches, I do not need to steam myself.

translation: "A Russian heart can even in the enemy of its fatherland distinguish a great man!" That is, to be honest, I don't recall if I actually expressed myself that way... I was a child... but the meaning was probably that! Napoleon was impressed; he pondered and said to his retinue: "I admire the pride of this child! But if all Russians think as this child does, then..." — he didn't finish his sentence and entered the palace. I immediately intervened in the retinue and ran after him. The retinue already parted before me and looked at me as if I were a favorite. But all of this was fleeting... I only remember that, entering the first hall, the emperor suddenly stopped before the portrait of Empress Catherine, looked at it thoughtfully for a long time, and finally said: "This was a great woman!" — and walked past. In two days, I was already known throughout the palace and the Kremlin, and they called me "le petit boyard." I only went home to sleep. At home, they almost went crazy. In two more days, Napoleon's chamberlain, Baron de Bazancur, died, unable to bear the campaign. Napoleon remembered me; they took me, led me in without explanation, dressed me in the uniform of the deceased, a boy of about twelve years old, and when they brought me in uniform to the emperor and he nodded at me with his head, they announced that I had been graciously promoted to the rank of chamberlain of his majesty. I was happy, I truly felt towards him, and for a long time already, a burning sympathy... well, and besides, you have to agree, a splendid uniform, which for a child constitutes a lot... I wore a dark green frock coat, with long, narrow skirts; golden buttons, red cuffs with gold embroidery, a high, standing, open collar, embroidered with gold, embroidery on the skirts; white tight-fitting breeches, a white silk waistcoat, silk stockings, shoes with buckles... and during the emperor's rides on horseback, and if I participated in the retinue, high riding boots. Although the position was not brilliant and huge misfortunes were already anticipated, etiquette was observed as much as possible, and even the more punctiliously, the stronger these misfortunes were anticipated.
source_text: «Русское сердце в состоянии даже в самом враге своего отечества отличить великого человека!». То есть, собственно, не помню, буквально ли я так выразился... я был ребенок... но смысл наверно был тот! Наполеон был поражен, он подумал и сказал своей свите: «Я люблю гордость этого ребенка! Но если все русские мыслят, как это дитя, то...» — он не договорил и вошел во дворец. Я тотчас же вмешался в свиту и побежал за ним. В свите уже расступались предо мной и смотрели на меня как на фаворита. Но всё это только мелькнуло... Помню только, что, войдя в первую залу, император вдруг остановился пред портретом императрицы Екатерины, долго, смотрел на него в задумчивости и наконец произнес: «Это была великая женщина!» — и прошел мимо. Чрез два дня меня все уже знали во дворце и в Кремле и звали «le petit boyard». Я только ночевать уходил домой. Дома чуть с ума не сошли. Наполеон вспомнил обо мне; меня взяли, привели, не объясняя дела, примерили на меня мундир покойного, мальчика лет двенадцати, и, когда уже привели меня в мундире к императору и он кивнул на меня головой, объявили мне, что я удостоен милостью и произведен в камер-пажи его величества. I was a child ... but the meaning must have been the same! Napoleon was amazed, he thought and said to his retinue: “I love the pride of this child! But if all Russians think like this child, then ... ”- he did not finish and entered the palace. I immediately intervened in the retinue and ran after him. The retinue already made way for me and looked at me as a favorite. But all this only flashed by... I only remember that, having entered the first hall, the emperor suddenly stopped in front of the portrait of Empress Catherine, looked at it for a long time in thought, and finally said: “That was a great woman!” — and passed by. Two days later, everyone in the palace and the Kremlin already knew me and called me "le petit boyard." I just went home for the night. The houses went a little crazy. Two days later, Napoleon's chamber page, Baron de Bazancourt, dies, unable to endure the campaign. Napoleon remembered me; They took me, brought me, without explaining the matter, tried on me the uniform of the deceased, a boy of about twelve years old, and when they had already brought me in uniform to the emperor and he nodded his head at me, they announced to me that I was honored with mercy and promoted to his chamber-page majesty. I was glad, I really felt for him, and for a long time already, a warm sympathy ... well, and besides, you will agree, a brilliant uniform, which is a lot for a child ... I went around in a dark green tailcoat, with long and narrow tails; gold buttons, red piping on sleeves with gold embroidery, high, standing, open collar, embroidered with gold, sewing on coattails; tight-fitting white leggings, a white silk waistcoat, silk stockings, shoes with buckles ... and during the emperor's walks on horseback, and if I participated in the retinue, high over the knee boots. Napoleon was astonished. He thought awhile and said to his suite. ‘I admire this boy’s pride! But if all Russians think like this lad, then…’ He did not finish and entered the Palace. I immediately mingled with his suite and ran after him. Members of his entourage parted to make way for me and treated me as their favourite. But all this was over in a flash… I merely remember that on entering the first hall, the Emperor stopped suddenly before a portrait of Empress Catherine, looked at it for a long time, lost in thought, and at last pronounced, ‘A grand lady indeed!’ and passed on. Two days later everyone knew me in the Palace and Kremlin and called me ‘le petit boyard’. * I used to go home only at night. At home people nearly went wild. In another two days Napoleon’s chamber page Baron de Bazancourt died without making it through the campaign. Napoleon remembered me. I was summoned, brought in without a word of explanation, told to put on the uniform of the deceased, a lad of about twelve and, after I was brought before the Emperor in my new outfit and he had given me a nod, was told I had been specially favoured and elevated to His Majesty’s chamber page. I was delighted. I really felt a strong attraction for him from the start… well, and on top of that there was the splendid uniform which meant so much to a young lad… I wore a dark green tailcoat with long, narrow flaps, gold buttons, red cuffs, stitched with gold thread, a high, stiff, open, gold-embroidered collar, the flaps being similarly decorated, tight-fitting, white, chamois leather pantaloons, a white silk vest, silk stockings, shoes with buckles… and when the Emperor went out riding, and I was included in his suite, I wore a pair of high riding boots. It was a dark green dress coat with gold buttons—red facings, white trousers, and a white silk waistcoat—silk stockings, shoes with buckles, and top-boots if I were riding out with his majesty or with the suite. "Though the position of all of us at that time was not particularly brilliant, and the poverty was dreadful all round, yet the etiquette at court was strictly preserved, and the more strictly in proportion to the growth of the forebodings of disaster."

translation: "A Russian heart is capable of recognizing even in the enemy of its homeland a great man!" Or, to be precise, I don't remember if I actually expressed myself like that... I was a child... but the meaning, I suppose, was that! Napoleon was struck, he pondered and said to his entourage, “I love the pride of this child! But if all Russians think as this child does, then…” — he didn't finish the sentence and entered the palace. I immediately intervened in the entourage and ran after him. They already parted before me in the entourage and looked at me as if I were a favorite. But all this just flashed by... I only remember that, entering the first hall, the emperor suddenly stopped in front of the portrait of Empress Catherine, looked at it thoughtfully for a long time and finally said, “This was a great woman!” — and walked on. Two days later, everyone already knew me in the palace and the Kremlin and called me "le petit boyard." I only went home to sleep. At home, they almost went mad. Two days later, Napoleon's chamberlain, Baron de Bazancourt, died, unable to bear the campaign. Napoleon remembered me; they took me, led me, without explaining the matter, put on me the uniform of the deceased, a boy of about twelve years old, and when they already brought me in uniform to the emperor and he nodded at me, they announced that I had been graced and promoted to the rank of chamberlain of his Majesty. I was happy, I truly felt towards him, and for a long time already, a burning sympathy... well, and besides, you agree, a brilliant uniform, which for a child is a big thing... I walked in a dark green frock coat, with long and narrow skirts; gold buttons, red cuffs with gold embroidery, a high, standing, open collar, embroidered with gold, embroidery on the skirts; white tight breeches, a white silk waistcoat, silk stockings, shoes with buckles... and during the emperor's horseback rides, and if I participated in the entourage, high riding boots. Although the position was not brilliant and great misfortunes were already foreseen, etiquette was observed as much as possible, and even the more punctually, the stronger these misfortunes were foreseen.
source_text: «Русское сердце в состоянии даже в самом враге своего отечества отличить великого человека!». То есть, собственно, не помню, буквально ли я так выразился... я был ребенок... но смысл наверно был тот! Наполеон был поражен, он подумал и сказал своей свите: «Я люблю гордость этого ребенка! Но если все русские мыслят, как это дитя, то...» — он не договорил и вошел во дворец. Я тотчас же вмешался в свиту и побежал за ним. В свите уже расступались предо мной и смотрели на меня как на фаворита. Но всё это только мелькнуло... Помню только, что, войдя в первую залу, император вдруг остановился пред портретом императрицы Екатерины, долго, смотрел на него в задумчивости и наконец произнес: «Это была великая женщина!» — и прошел мимо. Чрез два дня меня все уже знали во дворце и в Кремле и звали «le petit boyard». Я только ночевать уходил домой. Дома чуть с ума не сошли. Еще чрез два дня умирает камер-паж Наполеона, барон де Базанкур, не вынесший похода. Наполеон вспомнил обо мне; меня взяли, привели, не объясняя дела, примерили на меня мундир покойного, мальчика лет двенадцати, и, когда уже привели меня в мундире к императору и он кивнул на меня головой, объявили мне, что я удостоен милостью и произведен в камер-пажи его величества. Я был рад, я действительно чувствовал к нему, и давно уже, горячую симпатию... ну, и кроме того, согласитесь, блестящий мундир, что для ребенка составляет многое... Я ходил в темно-зеленом фраке, с длинными и узкими фалдами; золотые пуговицы, красные опушки на рукавах с золотым шитьем, высокий, стоячий, открытый воротник, шитый золотом, шитье на фалдах; белые лосинные панталоны в обтяжку, белый шелковый жилет, шелковые чулки, башмаки с пряжками... а во время прогулок императора на коне, и если я участвовал в свите, высокие ботфорты. Хотя положение было не блестящее и предчувствовались уже огромные бедствия, но этикет соблюдался по возможности, и даже тем пунктуальнее, чем сильнее предчувствовались эти бедствия.

human_translations.translator_1: To this instant question, I gave an instant reply, ‘A Russian deep in his heart can recognize a great man!’ Actually, to be perfectly frank, I don’t recall if that was word for word what I said… I was too young… but that was the gist of it! Napoleon was astonished. He thought awhile and said to his suite. ‘I admire this boy’s pride! But if all Russians think like this lad, then…’ He did not finish and entered the Palace. I immediately mingled with his suite and ran after him. Members of his entourage parted to make way for me and treated me as their favourite. But all this was over in a flash… I merely remember that on entering the first hall, the Emperor stopped suddenly before a portrait of Empress Catherine, looked at it for a long time, lost in thought, and at last pronounced, ‘A grand lady indeed!’ and passed on. Two days later everyone knew me in the Palace and Kremlin and called me ‘le petit boyard’. * I used to go home only at night. At home people nearly went wild. In another two days Napoleon’s chamber page Baron de Bazancourt died without making it through the campaign. Napoleon remembered me. I was summoned, brought in without a word of explanation, told to put on the uniform of the deceased, a lad of about twelve and, after I was brought before the Emperor in my new outfit and he had given me a nod, was told I had been specially favoured and elevated to His Majesty’s chamber page. I was delighted. I really felt a strong attraction for him from the start… well, and on top of that there was the splendid uniform which meant so much to a young lad… I wore a dark green tailcoat with long, narrow flaps, gold buttons, red cuffs, stitched with gold thread, a high, stiff, open, gold-embroidered collar, the flaps being similarly decorated, tight-fitting, white, chamois leather pantaloons, a white silk vest, silk stockings, shoes with buckles… and when the Emperor went out riding, and I was included in his suite, I wore a pair of high riding boots. Although the general situation was not brilliant to say the least and there was the whiff of enormous disaster in the air, etiquette was observed whenever possible and the more punctiliously, the closer disaster loomed.”
