He was extremely pleased to be accompanied by someone who was so learned and so pleasant - by this he meant K., who was occupied not with listening to the Italian but the director - and asked if he would be so kind, if the time was suitable, to meet him in the cathedral in two hours' time at about ten o'clock. He hoped he would certainly be able to be there at that time. K. made an appropriate reply, the Italian shook first the director's hand and then K.'s, then the director's again and went to the door, half turned to the two men who followed him and continuing to talk without a break. K. remained together with the director for a short while, although the director looked especially unhappy today. He thought he needed to apologise to K. for something and told him - they were standing intimately close together - he had thought at first he would accompany the Italian himself, but then - he gave no more precise reason than this - then he decided it would be better to send K. with him. He should not be surprised if he could not understand the Italian at first, he would be able to very soon, and even if he really could not understand very much he said it was not so bad, as it was really not so important for the Italian to be understood. And anyway, K.'s knowledge of Italian was surprisingly good, the director was sure he would get by very well. And with that, it was time for K. to go. He spent the time still remaining to him with a dictionary, copying out obscure words he would need to guide the Italian round the cathedral. It was an extremely irksome task, servitors brought him the mail, bank staff came with various queries and, when they saw that K. was busy, stood by the door and did not go away until he had listened to them, the deputy director did not miss the opportunity to disturb K. and came in frequently, took the dictionary from his hand and flicked through its pages, clearly for no purpose, when the door to the ante-room opened even clients would appear from the half darkness and bow timidly to him - they wanted to attract his attention but were not sure whether he had seen them - all this activity was circling around K. with him at its centre while he compiled the list of words he would need, then looked them up in the dictionary, then wrote them out, then practised their pronunciation and finally tried to learn them by heart. The good intentions he had had earlier, though, seemed to have left him completely, it was the Italian who had caused him all this effort and sometimes he became so angry with him that he buried the dictionary under some papers firmly intending to do no more preparation, but then he realised he could not walk up and down in the cathedral with the Italian without saying a word, so, in an even greater rage, he pulled the dictionary back out again.

translation: Right after the greetings – settling into the armchair, which K. invited him to do, he had no time – he asked K. for a short private conversation. "It's necessary," he said, swallowing with effort, "for my peace of mind, it's necessary." K. immediately sent the servants out of the room, with the instruction not to let anyone in. "What have I heard, Josef?" the uncle exclaimed when they were alone, sat down on the table, and stuffed various papers under himself, without looking, to sit better. K. was silent, he knew what was coming, but, suddenly relaxed from the strenuous work he had been doing, he initially gave himself over to a pleasant lethargy and looked out the window at the opposite side of the street, of which only a small, triangular section was visible from his seat, a piece of bare wall between two shop windows. "You're looking out the window!" the uncle called out with raised arms, "for heaven's sake, Josef, answer me! Is it true, can it really be true?" "Dear Uncle," said K., tearing himself from his distraction, "I don't even know what you want from me." "Josef," said the uncle warningly, "you've always told the truth, as far as I know. Should I take your last words as a bad omen?" "I guess I know what you want," said K. obediently, "you've probably heard about my trial." "That's right," replied the uncle, nodding slowly, "I've heard about your trial." "From whom?" asked K. "Erna wrote to me," said the uncle, "she doesn't have any contact with you, you don't care much for her, unfortunately, but she found out. Today I received the letter and naturally drove over immediately. For no other reason, but it seems like a sufficient reason. I can read you the passage of the letter that concerns you." He pulled the letter out of his wallet. "Here it is." She writes: 'Josef, I haven't seen you for a long time, last week I was once at the bank, but Josef was so busy that I wasn't allowed in; I waited for almost an hour, but then I had to go home because I had a piano lesson. I would have liked to speak to him, perhaps an opportunity will arise soon. For my name day, he sent me a large box of chocolates, it was very kind and thoughtful. I had forgotten to write to you about it back then, only now, since you are asking, do I remember. Chocolates, you must know, disappear from the boarding house immediately, as soon as one becomes aware that one has been gifted with chocolates, they are already gone. But as for Josef, I wanted to tell you something else. As mentioned, I wasn't allowed in to him at the bank because he was negotiating with a gentleman. After I had waited quietly for a while, I asked a servant if the negotiation would last long. He said that it probably would, because it was probably about the trial against the head clerk. I asked what kind of trial it was, if he wasn't mistaken, but he said he wasn't mistaken, it was a trial, and a serious one, he didn't know more. He himself would like to help the head clerk, because he is a good and just man, but he doesn't know how to start, and he just wishes that influential gentlemen would take over. This will certainly happen, and it will eventually have a good ending, but for now, as he could gather from the mood of the head clerk, it is not going well at all. I didn't pay much attention to this speech, of course, I also tried to reassure the simple servant, forbade him to talk about it to anyone else, and consider the whole thing as nonsense. Nevertheless, it might be good if you, dearest father, looked into the matter during your next visit, it will be easy for you to find out more and, if it really becomes necessary, to intervene with your great, influential acquaintances. Should it not be necessary, which is probably the most likely, then it will at least give your daughter the opportunity to hug you soon, which would make her happy.' – 'A good child,' said the uncle when he finished reading, and wiped away some tears. K. nodded, he had completely forgotten Erna due to the various disturbances of recent times, even her birthday had slipped his mind, and the story about the chocolate was apparently only invented to protect him from his uncle and aunt. It was very touching, and with the theatre tickets, which he intended to send her regularly from now on, certainly not sufficiently rewarded, but he didn't feel suited to visiting the boarding house and having conversations with an eighteen-year-old schoolgirl right now. "And what do you say now?" asked the uncle, who had forgotten all his haste and excitement through the letter and seemed to be reading it again. "Yes, Uncle," said K., "it's true." "True?" exclaimed the uncle.
source_text: Gleich nach der Begrüßung – sich in den Fauteuil zu setzen, wozu ihn K. einlud, hatte er keine Zeit – bat er K. um ein kurzes Gespräch unter vier Augen. »Es ist notwendig«, sagte er, mühselig schluckend, »zu meiner Beruhigung ist es notwendig.« K. schickte sofort die Diener aus dem Zimmer, mit der Weisung, niemand einzulassen. »Was habe ich gehört, Josef?« rief der Onkel, als sie allein waren, setzte sich auf den Tisch und stopfte unter sich, ohne hinzusehen, verschiedene Papiere, um besser zu sitzen. K. schwieg, er wußte, was kommen würde, aber, plötzlich von der anstrengenden Arbeit entspannt, wie er war, gab er sich zunächst einer angenehmen Mattigkeit hin und sah durch das Fenster auf die gegenüberliegende Straßenseite, von der von seinem Sitz aus nur ein kleiner, dreieckiger Ausschnitt zu sehen war, ein Stück leerer Häusermauer zwischen zwei Geschäftsauslagen. »Du schaust aus dem Fenster!« rief der Onkel mit erhobenen Armen, »um Himmels willen, Josef, antworte mir doch! Ist es wahr, kann es denn wahr sein?« »Lieber Onkel«, sagte K. und riß sich von seiner Zerstreutheit los, »ich weiß ja gar nicht, was du von mir willst.« »Josef«, sagte der Onkel warnend, »die Wahrheit hast du immer gesagt, soviel ich weiß. Soll ich deine letzten Worte als schlimmes Zeichen auffassen?« »Ich ahne ja, was du willst«, sagte K. folgsam, »du hast wahrscheinlich von meinem Prozeß gehört.« »So ist es«, antwortete der Onkel, langsam nickend, »ich habe von deinem Prozeß gehört.« »Von wem denn?« fragte K. »Erna hat es mir geschrieben«, sagte der Onkel, »sie hat ja keinen Verkehr mit dir, du kümmerst dich leider nicht viel um sie, trotzdem hat sie es erfahren. Heute habe ich den Brief bekommen und bin natürlich sofort hergefahren. Aus keinem anderen Grund, aber es scheint ein genügender Grund zu sein. Ich kann dir die Briefstelle, die dich betrifft, vorlesen.« Er zog den Brief aus der Brieftasche. »Hier ist es.« Sie schreibt: »Josef habe ich schon lange nicht gesehen, vorige Woche war ich einmal in der Bank, aber Josef war so beschäftigt, daß ich nicht vorgelassen wurde; ich habe fast eine Stunde gewartet, mußte dann aber nach Hause, weil ich Klavierstunde hatte. Ich hätte gern mit ihm gesprochen, vielleicht wird sich nächstens eine Gelegenheit finden. Zu meinem Namenstag hat er mir eine große Schachtel Schokolade geschickt, es war sehr lieb und aufmerksam. Ich hatte vergessen, es Euch damals zu schreiben, erst jetzt, da Ihr mich fragt, erinnere ich mich daran. Schokolade, müßt Ihr wissen, verschwindet nämlich in der Pension sofort, kaum ist man zum Bewußtsein dessen gekommen, daß man mit Schokolade beschenkt worden ist, ist sie auch schon weg. Aber was Josef betrifft, wollte ich Euch noch etwas sagen. Wie erwähnt, wurde ich in der Bank nicht zu ihm vorgelassen, weil er gerade mit einem Herrn verhandelte. Nachdem ich eine Zeitlang ruhig gewartet hatte, fragte ich einen Diener, ob die Verhandlung noch lange dauern werde. Er sagte, das dürfte wohl sein, denn es handle sich wahrscheinlich um den Prozeß, der gegen den Herrn Prokuristen geführt werde. Ich fragte, was denn das für ein Prozeß sei, ob er sich nicht irre, er aber sagte, er irre sich nicht, es sei ein Prozeß, und zwar ein schwerer Prozeß, mehr aber wisse er nicht. Er selbst möchte dem Herrn Prokuristen gerne helfen, denn dieser sei ein guter und gerechter Herr, aber er wisse nicht, wie er es anfangen sollte, und er möchte nur wünschen, daß sich einflußreiche Herren seiner annehmen würden. Dies werde auch sicher geschehen, und es werde schließlich ein gutes Ende nehmen, vorläufig aber stehe es, wie er aus der Laune des Herrn Prokuristen entnehmen könne, gar nicht gut. Ich legte diesen Reden natürlich nicht viel Bedeutung bei, suchte auch den einfältigen Diener zu beruhigen, verbot ihm, anderen gegenüber davon zu sprechen, und halte das Ganze für ein Geschwätz. Trotzdem wäre es vielleicht gut, wenn Du, liebster Vater, bei Deinem nächsten Besuch der Sache nachgehen wolltest, es wird Dir leicht sein, Genaueres zu erfahren und, wenn es wirklich nötig sein sollte, durch Deine großen, einflußreichen Bekanntschaften einzugreifen. Sollte es aber nicht nötig sein, was ja das wahrscheinlichste ist, so wird es wenigstens Deiner Tochter bald Gelegenheit geben, Dich zu umarmen, was sie freuen würde.‹ – Ein gutes Kind«, sagte der Onkel, als er die Vorlesung beendet hatte, und wischte einige Tränen aus den Augen fort. K. nickte, er hatte infolge der verschiedenen Störungen der letzten Zeit vollständig Erna vergessen, sogar ihren Geburtstag hatte er vergessen, und die Geschichte von der Schokolade war offenbar nur zu dem Zweck erfunden, um ihn vor Onkel und Tante in Schutz zu nehmen. Es war sehr rührend, und mit den Theaterkarten, die er ihr von jetzt ab regelmäßig schicken wollte, gewiß nicht genügend belohnt, aber zu Besuchen in der Pension und zu Unterhaltungen mit einer kleinen achtzehnjährigen Gymnasiastin fühlte er sich jetzt nicht geeignet. »Und was sagst du jetzt?« fragte der Onkel, der durch den Brief alle Eile und Aufregung vergessen hatte und ihn noch einmal zu lesen schien. »Ja, Onkel«, sagte K., »es ist wahr.« »Wahr?« rief der Onkel.

source_text: Gleich nach der Begrüßung – sich in den Fauteuil zu setzen, wozu ihn K. einlud, hatte er keine Zeit – bat er K. um ein kurzes Gespräch unter vier Augen. »Es ist notwendig«, sagte er, mühselig schluckend, »zu meiner Beruhigung ist es notwendig.« K. schickte sofort die Diener aus dem Zimmer, mit der Weisung, niemand einzulassen. »Was habe ich gehört, Josef?« rief der Onkel, als sie allein waren, setzte sich auf den Tisch und stopfte unter sich, ohne hinzusehen, verschiedene Papiere, um besser zu sitzen. K. schwieg, er wußte, was kommen würde, aber, plötzlich von der anstrengenden Arbeit entspannt, wie er war, gab er sich zunächst einer angenehmen Mattigkeit hin und sah durch das Fenster auf die gegenüberliegende Straßenseite, von der von seinem Sitz aus nur ein kleiner, dreieckiger Ausschnitt zu sehen war, ein Stück leerer Häusermauer zwischen zwei Geschäftsauslagen. »Du schaust aus dem Fenster!« rief der Onkel mit erhobenen Armen, »um Himmels willen, Josef, antworte mir doch! Ist es wahr, kann es denn wahr sein?« »Lieber Onkel«, sagte K. und riß sich von seiner Zerstreutheit los, »ich weiß ja gar nicht, was du von mir willst.« »Josef«, sagte der Onkel warnend, »die Wahrheit hast du immer gesagt, soviel ich weiß. Soll ich deine letzten Worte als schlimmes Zeichen auffassen?« »Ich ahne ja, was du willst«, sagte K. folgsam, »du hast wahrscheinlich von meinem Prozeß gehört.« »So ist es«, antwortete der Onkel, langsam nickend, »ich habe von deinem Prozeß gehört.« »Von wem denn?« fragte K. »Erna hat es mir geschrieben«, sagte der Onkel, »sie hat ja keinen Verkehr mit dir, du kümmerst dich leider nicht viel um sie, trotzdem hat sie es erfahren. Heute habe ich den Brief bekommen und bin natürlich sofort hergefahren. Aus keinem anderen Grund, aber es scheint ein genügender Grund zu sein. Ich kann dir die Briefstelle, die dich betrifft, vorlesen.« Er zog den Brief aus der Brieftasche. »Hier ist es.« Sie schreibt: »Josef habe ich schon lange nicht gesehen, vorige Woche war ich einmal in der Bank, aber Josef war so beschäftigt, daß ich nicht vorgelassen wurde; ich habe fast eine Stunde gewartet, mußte dann aber nach Hause, weil ich Klavierstunde hatte. Ich hätte gern mit ihm gesprochen, vielleicht wird sich nächstens eine Gelegenheit finden. Zu meinem Namenstag hat er mir eine große Schachtel Schokolade geschickt, es war sehr lieb und aufmerksam. Ich hatte vergessen, es Euch damals zu schreiben, erst jetzt, da Ihr mich fragt, erinnere ich mich daran. Schokolade, müßt Ihr wissen, verschwindet nämlich in der Pension sofort, kaum ist man zum Bewußtsein dessen gekommen, daß man mit Schokolade beschenkt worden ist, ist sie auch schon weg. Aber was Josef betrifft, wollte ich Euch noch etwas sagen. Wie erwähnt, wurde ich in der Bank nicht zu ihm vorgelassen, weil er gerade mit einem Herrn verhandelte. Nachdem ich eine Zeitlang ruhig gewartet hatte, fragte ich einen Diener, ob die Verhandlung noch lange dauern werde. Er sagte, das dürfte wohl sein, denn es handle sich wahrscheinlich um den Prozeß, der gegen den Herrn Prokuristen geführt werde. Ich fragte, was denn das für ein Prozeß sei, ob er sich nicht irre, er aber sagte, er irre sich nicht, es sei ein Prozeß, und zwar ein schwerer Prozeß, mehr aber wisse er nicht. Er selbst möchte dem Herrn Prokuristen gerne helfen, denn dieser sei ein guter und gerechter Herr, aber er wisse nicht, wie er es anfangen sollte, und er möchte nur wünschen, daß sich einflußreiche Herren seiner annehmen würden. Dies werde auch sicher geschehen, und es werde schließlich ein gutes Ende nehmen, vorläufig aber stehe es, wie er aus der Laune des Herrn Prokuristen entnehmen könne, gar nicht gut. Ich legte diesen Reden natürlich nicht viel Bedeutung bei, suchte auch den einfältigen Diener zu beruhigen, verbot ihm, anderen gegenüber davon zu sprechen, und halte das Ganze für ein Geschwätz. Trotzdem wäre es vielleicht gut, wenn Du, liebster Vater, bei Deinem nächsten Besuch der Sache nachgehen wolltest, es wird Dir leicht sein, Genaueres zu erfahren und, wenn es wirklich nötig sein sollte, durch Deine großen, einflußreichen Bekanntschaften einzugreifen. Sollte es aber nicht nötig sein, was ja das wahrscheinlichste ist, so wird es wenigstens Deiner Tochter bald Gelegenheit geben, Dich zu umarmen, was sie freuen würde.‹ – Ein gutes Kind«, sagte der Onkel, als er die Vorlesung beendet hatte, und wischte einige Tränen aus den Augen fort. K. nickte, er hatte infolge der verschiedenen Störungen der letzten Zeit vollständig Erna vergessen, sogar ihren Geburtstag hatte er vergessen, und die Geschichte von der Schokolade war offenbar nur zu dem Zweck erfunden, um ihn vor Onkel und Tante in Schutz zu nehmen. Es war sehr rührend, und mit den Theaterkarten, die er ihr von jetzt ab regelmäßig schicken wollte, gewiß nicht genügend belohnt, aber zu Besuchen in der Pension und zu Unterhaltungen mit einer kleinen achtzehnjährigen Gymnasiastin fühlte er sich jetzt nicht geeignet. »Und was sagst du jetzt?« fragte der Onkel, der durch den Brief alle Eile und Aufregung vergessen hatte und ihn noch einmal zu lesen schien. »Ja, Onkel«, sagte K., »es ist wahr.« »Wahr?« rief der Onkel.

translation: Right after the greeting – he hadn't had time to sit down in the armchair, which K. had invited him to – he asked K. for a brief private conversation. "It's necessary," he said, swallowing laboriously, "for my peace of mind, it's necessary." K. immediately sent the servants out of the room, with the instruction not to let anyone in. "What have I heard, Josef?" the uncle exclaimed, once they were alone, sat down on the table, and stuffed various papers under himself, without looking up, to sit more comfortably. K. was silent; he knew what was coming, but, suddenly relaxed from the strenuous work he had been doing, he gave himself over to a pleasant lethargy at first and looked out the window at the opposite side of the street, from his seat only a small, triangular section was visible, a piece of bare wall between two shop windows. "You are looking out the window!" the uncle exclaimed, raising his arms, "for heaven's sake, Josef, answer me! Is it true, can it really be true?" "Dear Uncle," said K. and pulled himself away from his distraction, "I don't even know what you want from me." "Josef," said the uncle warningly, "you've always told the truth, as far as I know. Should I take your last words as a bad omen?" "I guess I know what you want," said K. obediently, "you've probably heard about my trial." "That's it," replied the uncle, nodding slowly, "I heard about your trial." "From whom?" asked K. "Erna wrote to me," said the uncle, "she doesn't have any contact with you, you don't really care much about her, but she found out. Today I got the letter and naturally came right over. For no other reason, but it seems a sufficient one. I can read you the part of the letter that concerns you." He pulled the letter out of his wallet. "Here it is." She writes: "Josef, I haven't seen you in a long time, last week I was once at the bank, but Josef was so busy that I wasn't allowed in; I waited for almost an hour, but then I had to go home because I had a piano lesson. I would have liked to talk to him, maybe there will be an opportunity next time. For my name day he sent me a large box of chocolates, it was very kind and thoughtful. I had forgotten to write to you about it then, only now, since you are asking me, do I remember. You know, chocolates disappear from the pension immediately, as soon as one becomes aware that one has been gifted with chocolates, they are already gone. But about Josef, I wanted to tell you something else. As mentioned, I wasn't allowed in to see him at the bank because he was negotiating with a gentleman. After I had waited quietly for a while, I asked a servant whether the negotiations would last long. He said it probably would, because it was probably about the trial against Mr. Procurator. I asked what kind of trial it was, whether he wasn't mistaken, but he said he wasn't mistaken, it was a trial, and a serious one, but he didn't know any more. He himself would like to help Mr. Procurator, because he is a good and just man, but he didn't know how to start, and he only wished that influential gentlemen would take care of him. This would also surely happen, and it would eventually have a good ending, but provisionally it stood, as he could deduce from the mood of Mr. Procurator, not at all well. I didn't take much stock in this talk, of course, I also tried to reassure the naive servant, forbade him to talk about it to others, and consider the whole thing to be gossip. Nevertheless, it might be good if you, dearest father, looked into the matter during your next visit, it will be easy for you to find out more and, if it really becomes necessary, to intervene through your great, influential acquaintances. But should it not be necessary, which is probably the most likely, then it will at least give your daughter an opportunity to hug you soon, which would make her happy." – "A good child," said the uncle, when he had finished reading, and wiped some tears from his eyes. K. nodded; he had completely forgotten Erna because of the various disturbances of recent times, even her birthday had slipped his mind, and the story about the chocolates was apparently only invented in order to protect him in front of his uncle and aunt. It was very touching, and with the theater tickets that he would now regularly send her, certainly not adequately rewarded, but he didn't feel suited to visits to the pension and conversations with an eighteen-year-old schoolgirl right now. "And what do you say now?" asked the uncle, who had forgotten all haste and excitement through the letter and seemed to read it again. "Yes, Uncle," said K., "it is true." "True?" exclaimed the uncle.
source_text: Gleich nach der Begrüßung – sich in den Fauteuil zu setzen, wozu ihn K. einlud, hatte er keine Zeit – bat er K. um ein kurzes Gespräch unter vier Augen. »Es ist notwendig«, sagte er, mühselig schluckend, »zu meiner Beruhigung ist es notwendig.« K. schickte sofort die Diener aus dem Zimmer, mit der Weisung, niemand einzulassen. »Was habe ich gehört, Josef?« rief der Onkel, als sie allein waren, setzte sich auf den Tisch und stopfte unter sich, ohne hinzusehen, verschiedene Papiere, um besser zu sitzen. K. schwieg, er wußte, was kommen würde, aber, plötzlich von der anstrengenden Arbeit entspannt, wie er war, gab er sich zunächst einer angenehmen Mattigkeit hin und sah durch das Fenster auf die gegenüberliegende Straßenseite, von der von seinem Sitz aus nur ein kleiner, dreieckiger Ausschnitt zu sehen war, ein Stück leerer Häusermauer zwischen zwei Geschäftsauslagen. »Du schaust aus dem Fenster!« rief der Onkel mit erhobenen Armen, »um Himmels willen, Josef, antworte mir doch! Ist es wahr, kann es denn wahr sein?« »Lieber Onkel«, sagte K. und riß sich von seiner Zerstreutheit los, »ich weiß ja gar nicht, was du von mir willst.« »Josef«, sagte der Onkel warnend, »die Wahrheit hast du immer gesagt, soviel ich weiß. Soll ich deine letzten Worte als schlimmes Zeichen auffassen?« »Ich ahne ja, was du willst«, sagte K. folgsam, »du hast wahrscheinlich von meinem Prozeß gehört.« »So ist es«, antwortete der Onkel, langsam nickend, »ich habe von deinem Prozeß gehört.« »Von wem denn?« fragte K. »Erna hat es mir geschrieben«, sagte der Onkel, »sie hat ja keinen Verkehr mit dir, du kümmerst dich leider nicht viel um sie, trotzdem hat sie es erfahren. Heute habe ich den Brief bekommen und bin natürlich sofort hergefahren. Aus keinem anderen Grund, aber es scheint ein genügender Grund zu sein. Ich kann dir die Briefstelle, die dich betrifft, vorlesen.« Er zog den Brief aus der Brieftasche. »Hier ist es.« Sie schreibt: »Josef habe ich schon lange nicht gesehen, vorige Woche war ich einmal in der Bank, aber Josef war so beschäftigt, daß ich nicht vorgelassen wurde; ich habe fast eine Stunde gewartet, mußte dann aber nach Hause, weil ich Klavierstunde hatte. Ich hätte gern mit ihm gesprochen, vielleicht wird sich nächstens eine Gelegenheit finden. Zu meinem Namenstag hat er mir eine große Schachtel Schokolade geschickt, es war sehr lieb und aufmerksam. Ich hatte vergessen, es Euch damals zu schreiben, erst jetzt, da Ihr mich fragt, erinnere ich mich daran. Schokolade, müßt Ihr wissen, verschwindet nämlich in der Pension sofort, kaum ist man zum Bewußtsein dessen gekommen, daß man mit Schokolade beschenkt worden ist, ist sie auch schon weg. Aber was Josef betrifft, wollte ich Euch noch etwas sagen. Wie erwähnt, wurde ich in der Bank nicht zu ihm vorgelassen, weil er gerade mit einem Herrn verhandelte. Nachdem ich eine Zeitlang ruhig gewartet hatte, fragte ich einen Diener, ob die Verhandlung noch lange dauern werde. Er sagte, das dürfte wohl sein, denn es handle sich wahrscheinlich um den Prozeß, der gegen den Herrn Prokuristen geführt werde. Ich fragte, was denn das für ein Prozeß sei, ob er sich nicht irre, er aber sagte, er irre sich nicht, es sei ein Prozeß, und zwar ein schwerer Prozeß, mehr aber wisse er nicht. Er selbst möchte dem Herrn Prokuristen gerne helfen, denn dieser sei ein guter und gerechter Herr, aber er wisse nicht, wie er es anfangen sollte, und er möchte nur wünschen, daß sich einflußreiche Herren seiner annehmen würden. Dies werde auch sicher geschehen, und es werde schließlich ein gutes Ende nehmen, vorläufig aber stehe es, wie er aus der Laune des Herrn Prokuristen entnehmen könne, gar nicht gut. Ich legte diesen Reden natürlich nicht viel Bedeutung bei, suchte auch den einfältigen Diener zu beruhigen, verbot ihm, anderen gegenüber davon zu sprechen, und halte das Ganze für ein Geschwätz. Trotzdem wäre es vielleicht gut, wenn Du, liebster Vater, bei Deinem nächsten Besuch der Sache nachgehen wolltest, es wird Dir leicht sein, Genaueres zu erfahren und, wenn es wirklich nötig sein sollte, durch Deine großen, einflußreichen Bekanntschaften einzugreifen. Sollte es aber nicht nötig sein, was ja das wahrscheinlichste ist, so wird es wenigstens Deiner Tochter bald Gelegenheit geben, Dich zu umarmen, was sie freuen würde.‹ – Ein gutes Kind«, sagte der Onkel, als er die Vorlesung beendet hatte, und wischte einige Tränen aus den Augen fort. K. nickte, er hatte infolge der verschiedenen Störungen der letzten Zeit vollständig Erna vergessen, sogar ihren Geburtstag hatte er vergessen, und die Geschichte von der Schokolade war offenbar nur zu dem Zweck erfunden, um ihn vor Onkel und Tante in Schutz zu nehmen. Es war sehr rührend, und mit den Theaterkarten, die er ihr von jetzt ab regelmäßig schicken wollte, gewiß nicht genügend belohnt, aber zu Besuchen in der Pension und zu Unterhaltungen mit einer kleinen achtzehnjährigen Gymnasiastin fühlte er sich jetzt nicht geeignet. »Und was sagst du jetzt?« fragte der Onkel, der durch den Brief alle Eile und Aufregung vergessen hatte und ihn noch einmal zu lesen schien. »Ja, Onkel«, sagte K., »es ist wahr.« »Wahr?« rief der Onkel.

After I had waited meekly for a while I asked an attendant if the interview was likely to last much longer. He said that that might very well be, for it had probably something to do with the case which was being brought against the Chief Clerk. I asked what case, and was he not mistaken, but he said he was not mistaken, there was a case and a very serious one too, but more than that he did not know. translation: Right after the greeting – he was invited to sit down in an armchair, but didn't have time – he asked K. for a short private conversation. "It's necessary," he said, swallowing with effort, "for my own peace of mind, it's necessary." K. immediately sent the servants out of the room, with instructions not to let anyone in. "What have I heard, Josef?" the uncle exclaimed, once they were alone, sat down on the table, and shoved various papers under himself without looking, to sit more comfortably. K. remained silent; he knew what was coming, but, suddenly relaxed from the demanding work he had been doing, he surrendered to a pleasant drowsiness and looked out the window at the opposite street, of which only a small triangular section was visible from his seat, a piece of bare wall between two shop windows. "You're looking out the window!" the uncle cried, raising his arms, "For heaven's sake, Josef, answer me! Is it true, can it possibly be true?" "Dear Uncle," said K., tearing himself away from his distraction, "I don't even know what you want from me." "Josef," the uncle said warningly, "you've always told the truth, as far as I know. Should I interpret your last words as a bad omen?" "I guess I know what you want," said K. obediently, "you've probably heard about my trial." "That's right," the uncle answered, slowly nodding, "I've heard about your trial." "From whom?" asked K. "Erna wrote to me," said the uncle, "she doesn't have much contact with you, you don't pay much attention to her, unfortunately, but she found out. I got the letter today and naturally came straight here. For no other reason, but it seems a sufficient one. I can read you the passage that concerns you." He pulled the letter out of his wallet. "Here it is." He began to read: "Josef, I haven't seen you for a long time. Last week I went to the bank once, but Josef was so busy that I wasn't allowed in; I had to wait for almost an hour, but then I had to go home because I had a piano lesson. I would have liked to speak with him, perhaps there will be an opportunity next time. For my name day he sent me a large box of chocolates, it was very kind and thoughtful. I had forgotten to write to you about it then, only now, since you are asking me, do I remember. Chocolates, you must know, disappear from the pension immediately, as soon as one becomes aware that one has been gifted with chocolates, they are already gone. But about Josef, I wanted to tell you something else. As mentioned, I was not allowed to see him in the bank because he was negotiating with a gentleman. After I had waited quietly for a while, I asked a servant if the negotiation would last long. He said it probably would, because it was probably about the trial against the head clerk. I asked what kind of trial it was, whether he was mistaken, but he said he was not mistaken, it was a trial, and a serious one, but he didn't know any more. He himself would like to help the head clerk, because he is a good and just man, but he doesn't know how to start, and he only wishes that influential gentlemen would take his case. This will certainly happen, and it will eventually have a good ending, but for the time being, as he can tell from the mood of the head clerk, it is not looking good at all. I did not attach much importance to this speech, of course, I also tried to reassure the simple servant, forbade him to speak about it to others, and consider the whole thing as nonsense. Nevertheless, it might be good if you, dearest father, would look into the matter during your next visit, it will be easy for you to find out more and, if it really is necessary, to intervene with your great, influential acquaintances. Should it not be necessary, which is probably the most likely, then it will at least soon give your daughter the opportunity to hug you, which would please her." "A good child," said the uncle, when he had finished reading, and wiped some tears from his eyes. K. nodded; as a result of the various disruptions of the last few weeks, he had completely forgotten about Erna, he had even forgotten her birthday, and the story about the chocolates was apparently only invented to protect him from his uncle and aunt. It was very touching, and with the theatre tickets that he wanted to send her regularly from now on, certainly not adequately rewarded, but visits to the pension and conversations with an eighteen-year-old schoolgirl did not feel right to him at the moment. "And what do you say now?" asked the uncle, who had forgotten all haste and excitement thanks to the letter and seemed to be reading it again. "Yes, Uncle," said K., "it's true." "True?" the uncle exclaimed.
source_text: Gleich nach der Begrüßung – sich in den Fauteuil zu setzen, wozu ihn K. einlud, hatte er keine Zeit – bat er K. um ein kurzes Gespräch unter vier Augen. »Es ist notwendig«, sagte er, mühselig schluckend, »zu meiner Beruhigung ist es notwendig.« K. schickte sofort die Diener aus dem Zimmer, mit der Weisung, niemand einzulassen. »Was habe ich gehört, Josef?« rief der Onkel, als sie allein waren, setzte sich auf den Tisch und stopfte unter sich, ohne hinzusehen, verschiedene Papiere, um besser zu sitzen. K. schwieg, er wußte, was kommen würde, aber, plötzlich von der anstrengenden Arbeit entspannt, wie er war, gab er sich zunächst einer angenehmen Mattigkeit hin und sah durch das Fenster auf die gegenüberliegende Straßenseite, von der von seinem Sitz aus nur ein kleiner, dreieckiger Ausschnitt zu sehen war, ein Stück leerer Häusermauer zwischen zwei Geschäftsauslagen. »Du schaust aus dem Fenster!« rief der Onkel mit erhobenen Armen, »um Himmels willen, Josef, antworte mir doch! Ist es wahr, kann es denn wahr sein?« »Lieber Onkel«, sagte K. und riß sich von seiner Zerstreutheit los, »ich weiß ja gar nicht, was du von mir willst.« »Josef«, sagte der Onkel warnend, »die Wahrheit hast du immer gesagt, soviel ich weiß. Soll ich deine letzten Worte als schlimmes Zeichen auffassen?« »Ich ahne ja, was du willst«, sagte K. folgsam, »du hast wahrscheinlich von meinem Prozeß gehört.« »So ist es«, antwortete der Onkel, langsam nickend, »ich habe von deinem Prozeß gehört.« »Von wem denn?« fragte K. »Erna hat es mir geschrieben«, sagte der Onkel, »sie hat ja keinen Verkehr mit dir, du kümmerst dich leider nicht viel um sie, trotzdem hat sie es erfahren. Heute habe ich den Brief bekommen und bin natürlich sofort hergefahren. Aus keinem anderen Grund, aber es scheint ein genügender Grund zu sein. Ich kann dir die Briefstelle, die dich betrifft, vorlesen.« Er zog den Brief aus der Brieftasche. »Hier ist es.« Sie schreibt: »Josef habe ich schon lange nicht gesehen, vorige Woche war ich einmal in der Bank, aber Josef war so beschäftigt, daß ich nicht vorgelassen wurde; ich habe fast eine Stunde gewartet, mußte dann aber nach Hause, weil ich Klavierstunde hatte. Ich hätte gern mit ihm gesprochen, vielleicht wird sich nächstens eine Gelegenheit finden. Zu meinem Namenstag hat er mir eine große Schachtel Schokolade geschickt, es war sehr lieb und aufmerksam. Ich hatte vergessen, es Euch damals zu schreiben, erst jetzt, da Ihr mich fragt, erinnere ich mich daran. Schokolade, müßt Ihr wissen, verschwindet nämlich in der Pension sofort, kaum ist man zum Bewußtsein dessen gekommen, daß man mit Schokolade beschenkt worden ist, ist sie auch schon weg. Aber was Josef betrifft, wollte ich Euch noch etwas sagen. Wie erwähnt, wurde ich in der Bank nicht zu ihm vorgelassen, weil er gerade mit einem Herrn verhandelte. Nachdem ich eine Zeitlang ruhig gewartet hatte, fragte ich einen Diener, ob die Verhandlung noch lange dauern werde. Er sagte, das dürfte wohl sein, denn es handle sich wahrscheinlich um den Prozeß, der gegen den Herrn Prokuristen geführt werde. Ich fragte, was denn das für ein Prozeß sei, ob er sich nicht irre, er aber sagte, er irre sich nicht, es sei ein Prozeß, und zwar ein schwerer Prozeß, mehr aber wisse er nicht. Er selbst möchte dem Herrn Prokuristen gerne helfen, denn dieser sei ein guter und gerechter Herr, aber er wisse nicht, wie er es anfangen sollte, und er möchte nur wünschen, daß sich einflußreiche Herren seiner annehmen würden. Dies werde auch sicher geschehen, und es werde schließlich ein gutes Ende nehmen, vorläufig aber stehe es, wie er aus der Laune des Herrn Prokuristen entnehmen könne, gar nicht gut. Ich legte diesen Reden natürlich nicht viel Bedeutung bei, suchte auch den einfältigen Diener zu beruhigen, verbot ihm, anderen gegenüber davon zu sprechen, und halte das Ganze für ein Geschwätz. Trotzdem wäre es vielleicht gut, wenn Du, liebster Vater, bei Deinem nächsten Besuch der Sache nachgehen wolltest, es wird Dir leicht sein, Genaueres zu erfahren und, wenn es wirklich nötig sein sollte, durch Deine großen, einflußreichen Bekanntschaften einzugreifen. Sollte es aber nicht nötig sein, was ja das wahrscheinlichste ist, so wird es wenigstens Deiner Tochter bald Gelegenheit geben, Dich zu umarmen, was sie freuen würde.‹ – Ein gutes Kind«, sagte der Onkel, als er die Vorlesung beendet hatte, und wischte einige Tränen aus den Augen fort. K. nickte, er hatte infolge der verschiedenen Störungen der letzten Zeit vollständig Erna vergessen, sogar ihren Geburtstag hatte er vergessen, und die Geschichte von der Schokolade war offenbar nur zu dem Zweck erfunden, um ihn vor Onkel und Tante in Schutz zu nehmen. Es war sehr rührend, und mit den Theaterkarten, die er ihr von jetzt ab regelmäßig schicken wollte, gewiß nicht genügend belohnt, aber zu Besuchen in der Pension und zu Unterhaltungen mit einer kleinen achtzehnjährigen Gymnasiastin fühlte er sich jetzt nicht geeignet. »Und was sagst du jetzt?« fragte der Onkel, der durch den Brief alle Eile und Aufregung vergessen hatte und ihn noch einmal zu lesen schien. »Ja, Onkel«, sagte K., »es ist wahr.« »Wahr?« rief der Onkel.

K. said nothing. I can read you the passage that concerns you.” He pulled the letter from his wallet. “Here it is. She writes: ‘It’s been a long time since I’ve seen Josef, I was in the bank once last week, but Josef was so busy I couldn’t see him ; I waited for over an hour, but then I had to return home for my piano lesson. I forgot to write you about it earlier, and only remembered when you asked me. As I’m sure you know, chocolate disappears instantly at the boardinghouse, you hardly realize you’ve been given chocolates and they’re gone. But regarding Josef, there’s something else I wanted to tell you: As I mentioned, I couldn’t get in to see him because he was busy with a gentleman. After I’d waited patiently for a while, I asked an assistant whether the appointment would last much longer. He said that it might, since it probably had something to do with the trial the chief financial officer was involved in. I asked what sort of a trial it was, whether he might be mistaken, but he said it was no mistake, it was a trial and a serious one at that, but that’s all he knew. He said he’d like to help the chief financial officer himself, because he was a good and honest man, but he didn’t know how to go about it, and he could only hope that influential people would intervene in his behalf. He thought that would surely happen and that things would turn out well, but for the moment, as he gathered from the chief financial officer’s mood, things didn’t look at all good. "It's necessary," he said, swallowing with effort, "for my peace of mind, it's necessary." K. immediately sent the servants out of the room, with instructions not to let anyone in. "What have I heard, Josef?" cried the uncle, once they were alone, sat down on the table and, without looking up, stuffed various papers under himself to sit more comfortably. K. was silent; he knew what was coming, but, suddenly relaxed from the exhausting work he had been doing, he at first surrendered to a pleasant lethargy and looked out the window at the opposite side of the street, which, from his seat, offered only a small, triangular glimpse – a piece of bare wall between two shop windows. Should I take your last words as a bad omen?" "I guess I know what you want," said K. obediently, "you've probably heard about my trial." "Erna wrote to me," said the uncle, "she doesn't have much contact with you, you unfortunately don't care much for her, but she found out. Today I received the letter and, of course, came immediately. For no other reason, but it seems to be a sufficient one. I can read you the passage that concerns you." I would have liked to speak to him, perhaps there will be an opportunity next time. For my name day he sent me a large box of chocolates, it was very kind and thoughtful. Chocolates, you must know, disappear immediately in the pension, as soon as one becomes aware that one has been given chocolates, they are already gone. But about Josef, I wanted to tell you something else. As mentioned, I wasn't allowed to him in the bank because he was negotiating with a gentleman. After I had waited quietly for a while, I asked a servant if the negotiations would last long. He said that it probably would, because it was probably about the trial against the procurator. I asked what kind of trial it was, if he wasn't mistaken, but he said he wasn't mistaken, it was a trial, and a serious one, he didn't know any more. source_text: Gleich nach der Begrüßung – sich in den Fauteuil zu setzen, wozu ihn K. einlud, hatte er keine Zeit – bat er K. um ein kurzes Gespräch unter vier Augen. »Es ist notwendig«, sagte er, mühselig schluckend, »zu meiner Beruhigung ist es notwendig.« K. schickte sofort die Diener aus dem Zimmer, mit der Weisung, niemand einzulassen. »Was habe ich gehört, Josef?« rief der Onkel, als sie allein waren, setzte sich auf den Tisch und stopfte unter sich, ohne hinzusehen, verschiedene Papiere, um besser zu sitzen. K. schwieg, er wußte, was kommen würde, aber, plötzlich von der anstrengenden Arbeit entspannt, wie er war, gab er sich zunächst einer angenehmen Mattigkeit hin und sah durch das Fenster auf die gegenüberliegende Straßenseite, von der von seinem Sitz aus nur ein kleiner, dreieckiger Ausschnitt zu sehen war, ein Stück leerer Häusermauer zwischen zwei Geschäftsauslagen. »Du schaust aus dem Fenster!« rief der Onkel mit erhobenen Armen, »um Himmels willen, Josef, antworte mir doch! Ist es wahr, kann es denn wahr sein?« »Lieber Onkel«, sagte K. und riß sich von seiner Zerstreutheit los, »ich weiß ja gar nicht, was du von mir willst.« »Josef«, sagte der Onkel warnend, »die Wahrheit hast du immer gesagt, soviel ich weiß. Soll ich deine letzten Worte als schlimmes Zeichen auffassen?« »Ich ahne ja, was du willst«, sagte K. folgsam, »du hast wahrscheinlich von meinem Prozeß gehört.« »So ist es«, antwortete der Onkel, langsam nickend, »ich habe von deinem Prozeß gehört.« »Von wem denn?« fragte K. »Erna hat es mir geschrieben«, sagte der Onkel, »sie hat ja keinen Verkehr mit dir, du kümmerst dich leider nicht viel um sie, trotzdem hat sie es erfahren. Heute habe ich den Brief bekommen und bin natürlich sofort hergefahren. Aus keinem anderen Grund, aber es scheint ein genügender Grund zu sein. Ich kann dir die Briefstelle, die dich betrifft, vorlesen.« Er zog den Brief aus der Brieftasche. »Hier ist es.« Sie schreibt: »Josef habe ich schon lange nicht gesehen, vorige Woche war ich einmal in der Bank, aber Josef war so beschäftigt, daß ich nicht vorgelassen wurde; ich habe fast eine Stunde gewartet, mußte dann aber nach Hause, weil ich Klavierstunde hatte. Ich hätte gern mit ihm gesprochen, vielleicht wird sich nächstens eine Gelegenheit finden. Zu meinem Namenstag hat er mir eine große Schachtel Schokolade geschickt, es war sehr lieb und aufmerksam. Ich hatte vergessen, es Euch damals zu schreiben, erst jetzt, da Ihr mich fragt, erinnere ich mich daran. Schokolade, müßt Ihr wissen, verschwindet nämlich in der Pension sofort, kaum ist man zum Bewußtsein dessen gekommen, daß man mit Schokolade beschenkt worden ist, ist sie auch schon weg. Aber was Josef betrifft, wollte ich Euch noch etwas sagen. Wie erwähnt, wurde ich in der Bank nicht zu ihm vorgelassen, weil er gerade mit einem Herrn verhandelte. Nachdem ich eine Zeitlang ruhig gewartet hatte, fragte ich einen Diener, ob die Verhandlung noch lange dauern werde. Er sagte, das dürfte wohl sein, denn es handle sich wahrscheinlich um den Prozeß, der gegen den Herrn Prokuristen geführt werde. Ich fragte, was denn das für ein Prozeß sei, ob er sich nicht irre, er aber sagte, er irre sich nicht, es sei ein Prozeß, und zwar ein schwerer Prozeß, mehr aber wisse er nicht. Er selbst möchte dem Herrn Prokuristen gerne helfen, denn dieser sei ein guter und gerechter Herr, aber er wisse nicht, wie er es anfangen sollte, und er möchte nur wünschen, daß sich einflußreiche Herren seiner annehmen würden. Dies werde auch sicher geschehen, und es werde schließlich ein gutes Ende nehmen, vorläufig aber stehe es, wie er aus der Laune des Herrn Prokuristen entnehmen könne, gar nicht gut. Ich legte diesen Reden natürlich nicht viel Bedeutung bei, suchte auch den einfältigen Diener zu beruhigen, verbot ihm, anderen gegenüber davon zu sprechen, und halte das Ganze für ein Geschwätz. Trotzdem wäre es vielleicht gut, wenn Du, liebster Vater, bei Deinem nächsten Besuch der Sache nachgehen wolltest, es wird Dir leicht sein, Genaueres zu erfahren und, wenn es wirklich nötig sein sollte, durch Deine großen, einflußreichen Bekanntschaften einzugreifen. Sollte es aber nicht nötig sein, was ja das wahrscheinlichste ist, so wird es wenigstens Deiner Tochter bald Gelegenheit geben, Dich zu umarmen, was sie freuen würde.‹ – Ein gutes Kind«, sagte der Onkel, als er die Vorlesung beendet hatte, und wischte einige Tränen aus den Augen fort. K. nickte, er hatte infolge der verschiedenen Störungen der letzten Zeit vollständig Erna vergessen, sogar ihren Geburtstag hatte er vergessen, und die Geschichte von der Schokolade war offenbar nur zu dem Zweck erfunden, um ihn vor Onkel und Tante in Schutz zu nehmen. Es war sehr rührend, und mit den Theaterkarten, die er ihr von jetzt ab regelmäßig schicken wollte, gewiß nicht genügend belohnt, aber zu Besuchen in der Pension und zu Unterhaltungen mit einer kleinen achtzehnjährigen Gymnasiastin fühlte er sich jetzt nicht geeignet. »Und was sagst du jetzt?« fragte der Onkel, der durch den Brief alle Eile und Aufregung vergessen hatte und ihn noch einmal zu lesen schien. »Ja, Onkel«, sagte K., »es ist wahr.« »Wahr?« rief der Onkel.

translation: Nobody paid any attention to him, though. The family was completely absorbed in the violin playing; the lodgers, who at first, with their hands in their pockets, had positioned themselves far too close behind the sister's music stand, so that they could all see the notes—which must have been a nuisance to her—soon withdrew to the window with half-whispered conversations and heads bowed. The father watched them with evident concern, and they stayed there. It really seemed as though, disappointed in their assumption of hearing beautiful or entertaining music, they were tired of the whole performance and only allowed themselves to be disturbed in their tranquility out of politeness. Especially the way they all puffed smoke from their cigars upwards from their noses and mouths gave an impression of great nervousness. And yet, the sister played so beautifully. Her face was tilted to the side, her gaze searching and sad, following the lines of the notes. Gregor crept a little further forward and held his head close to the floor, hoping perhaps to meet her gaze. Was he an animal, to be so moved by music? It felt as if the path to the longed-for, unknown nourishment was being shown to him. He was determined to push his way to his sister, to tug at her skirt and thereby hint to her that she should come into his room with her violin, for no one here deserved her music as he did. He didn't want to let her out of his room anymore, at least not as long as he lived; his frightening form would be useful to him for the first time; he wanted to be at all the doors of his room at once, barking at the attackers; but his sister should stay with him voluntarily; she should sit next to him on the sofa, lean her ear to him, and he would then confide in her that he had the firm intention of sending her to the Conservatory, and that he would have told everyone that, if not for the misfortune that had intervened, last Christmas—Christmas was surely over by now?—without paying any attention to any objections. After this explanation, the sister would burst into tears of emotion, and Gregor would rise up to her shoulder and kiss her neck, which she had been wearing free of any collar or band since she started working.
source_text: Allerdings achtete auch niemand auf ihn. Die Familie war gänzlich vom Violinspiel in Anspruch genommen; die Zimmerherren dagegen, die zunächst, die Hände in den Hosentaschen, viel zu nahe hinter dem Notenpult der Schwester sich aufgestellt hatten, so daß sie alle in die Noten hätte sehen können, was sicher die Schwester stören mußte, zogen sich bald unter halblauten Gesprächen mit gesenkten Köpfen zum Fenster zurück, wo sie, vom Vater besorgt beobachtet, auch blieben. Es hatte nun wirklich den überdeutlichen Anschein, als wären sie in ihrer Annahme, ein schönes oder unterhaltendes Violinspiel zu hören, enttäuscht, hätten die ganze Vorführung satt und ließen sich nur aus Höflichkeit noch in ihrer Ruhe stören. Besonders die Art, wie sie alle aus Nase und Mund den Rauch ihrer Zigarren in die Höhe bliesen, ließ auf große Nervosität schließen. Und doch spielte die Schwester so schön. Ihr Gesicht war zur Seite geneigt, prüfend und traurig folgten ihre Blicke den Notenzeilen. Gregor kroch noch ein Stück vorwärts und hielt den Kopf eng an den Boden, um möglicherweise ihren Blicken begegnen zu können. War er ein Tier, da ihn Musik so ergriff? Ihm war, als zeige sich ihm der Weg zu der ersehnten unbekannten Nahrung. Er war entschlossen, bis zur Schwester vorzudringen, sie am Rock zu zupfen und ihr dadurch anzudeuten, sie möge doch mit ihrer Violine in sein Zimmer kommen, denn niemand lohnte hier das Spiel so, wie er es lohnen wollte. Er wollte sie nicht mehr aus seinem Zimmer lassen, wenigstens nicht, solange er lebte; seine Schreckgestalt sollte ihm zum erstenmal nützlich werden; an allen Türen seines Zimmers wollte er gleichzeitig sein und den Angreifern entgegenfauchen; die Schwester aber sollte nicht gezwungen, sondern freiwillig bei ihm bleiben; sie sollte neben ihm auf dem Kanapee sitzen, das Ohr zu ihm herunterneigen, und er wollte ihr dann anvertrauen, daß er die feste Absicht gehabt habe, sie auf das Konservatorium zu schicken, und daß er dies, wenn nicht das Unglück dazwischen gekommen wäre, vergangene Weihnachten – Weihnachten war doch wohl schon vorüber? – allen gesagt hätte, ohne sich um irgendwelche Widerreden zu kümmern. Nach dieser Erklärung würde die Schwester in Tränen der Rührung ausbrechen, und Gregor würde sich bis zu ihrer Achsel erheben und ihren Hals küssen, den sie, seitdem sie ins Geschäft ging, frei ohne Band oder Kragen trug.

After this declaration, his sister would be moved to the point of tears, and Gregor would raise himself to the height of her armpit and kiss her throat, which, now that she went to the office every day, she wore free of ribbon or collar.

translation: No one paid any attention to him, however. The family was entirely absorbed in the violin playing; the lodgers, who at first, with their hands in their pockets, had stood much too close behind the sister's music stand, so that they could have all seen the notes, which must certainly have bothered her, soon withdrew to the window, engaged in half-whispered conversations with their heads bowed. There they remained, observed by their father from a distance, as if disappointed in their expectation of hearing beautiful or entertaining music, having had quite enough of the performance, and letting themselves only be disturbed in their repose out of politeness. Especially the way they all blew smoke from their cigars upwards from nose and mouth hinted at great nervousness. And yet the sister played so beautifully. Her face was tilted to the side, her eyes followed the lines of music with a scrutinizing and mournful gaze. Gregor crawled forward a bit more and pressed his head close to the ground, hoping to be able to meet her gaze. Was he an animal, that music affected him so deeply? It felt as if the way to the desired, unknown nourishment were revealed to him. He was determined to push forward to his sister, to tug at her dress and thereby signal to her to come to his room with her violin, for no one here deserved her playing as he did. He didn't want to let her out of his room again, at least not as long as he lived; his frightful form should be of use to him for the first time; he wanted to be at all the doors of his room simultaneously, to snarl at attackers; but the sister should stay with him voluntarily; she should sit beside him on the couch, lean her ear towards him, and he would confide in her that he had always intended to send her to the conservatory, and that he would have told everyone this last Christmas – Christmas was over, wasn't it? – without paying any attention to any objections. After this explanation, the sister would burst into tears of emotion, and Gregor would rise up to her shoulder and kiss her neck, which she had worn free of collar or tie ever since she started working.

translation: Heidi had probably waited ten minutes and looked around on all sides to see if the children with the goats were anywhere in sight.  As they weren't, she climbed a little higher, so that she could better oversee the entire meadow, and from there she looked back and forth with signs of great impatience on her face and in her movements. Meanwhile, the children approached on a long detour, because Peter knew many places where there were all sorts of good things for his goats to nibble on in the bushes and shrubs; therefore he made many turns on the path with his flock. At first, the child had climbed wearily, panting from the heat and discomfort in his heavy armor, straining every muscle. He didn't say a word, but looked uncomprehendingly first at Peter, who with his bare feet and light trousers jumped back and forth effortlessly, and then at the goats, who with their thin, slender legs climbed even more easily over bushes and stones and steep slopes.  Suddenly the child sat down on the ground, quickly took off his shoes and socks, stood up again, pulled his red, thick scarf away, opened his petticoat, quickly pulled it off, and had to unhook another one because Base Dete had put on his Sunday dress over his everyday clothes out of haste so that no one had to wear it.  As quickly as that, the everyday petticoat was gone too, and now the child stood in its light under-petticoat, its bare arms joyously stretching out of the short shirt sleeves. Then he neatly placed everything in a pile, and now he sprang and climbed after the goats and beside Peter, as light as one of the whole company. Peter hadn't paid attention to what the child was doing while it was left behind. As it now came bounding up in its new clothes, he grinned broadly and stretched his whole face, and when he saw the pile of clothes lying below, his face spread even wider, and his mouth almost went from ear to ear; but he said nothing. Since the child felt so free and light, it started a conversation with Peter, and he also began to talk and had to answer many questions because the child wanted to know how many goats he had, where he was going with them, and what he would do when he arrived.  Finally, the children, along with the goats, reached the hut and came face to face with Base Dete. As soon as she saw the approaching company, she cried out loudly: "Heidi, what are you doing? What do you look like? Where is your skirt and your second one and your scarf? And I bought you brand new shoes for the mountain and made you new socks, and all gone! All gone! Heidi, what are you doing, where is everything?"
source_text: Die Dete hatte wohl zehn Minuten gewartet und sich nach allen Seiten umgesehen, ob die Kinder mit den Geißen noch nirgends zu sehen seien; als dies aber nicht der Fall war, so stieg sie noch ein wenig höher, wo sie besser die ganze Alm bis hinunter übersehen konnte, und guckte nun von hier aus bald dahin, bald dorthin mit Zeichen großer Ungeduld auf dem Gesicht und in den Bewegungen. Unterdessen rückten die Kinder auf einem großen Umwege heran, denn der Peter wusste viele Stellen, wo allerhand Gutes an Sträuchern und Gebüschen für seine Geißen zu nagen war; darum machte er mit seiner Herde vielerlei Wendungen auf dem Wege. Erst war das Kind mühsam nachgeklettert, in seiner schweren Rüstung vor Hitze und Unbequemlichkeit keuchend und alle Kräfte anstrengend. Es sagte kein Wort, blickte aber unverwandt bald auf den Peter, der mit seinen nackten Füßen und leichten Höschen ohne alle Mühe hin und her sprang, bald auf die Geißen, die mit den dünnen, schlanken Beinchen noch leichter über Busch und Stein und steile Abhänge hinaufkletterten. Auf einmal setzte das Kind sich auf den Boden nieder, zog mit großer Schnelligkeit Schuhe und Strümpfe aus, stand wieder auf, zog sein rotes, dickes Halstuch weg, machte sein Röckchen auf, zog es schnell aus und hatte gleich noch eins auszuhäkeln, denn die Base Dete hatte ihm das Sonntagskleidchen über das Alltagszeug angezogen, um der Kürze willen, damit niemand es tragen müsse. Blitzschnell war auch das Alltagsröcklein weg, und nun stand das Kind im leichten Unterröckchen, die bloßen Arme aus den kurzen Hemdärmelchen vergnüglich in die Luft hinausstreckend. Dann legte es schön alles auf ein Häufchen, und nun sprang und kletterte es hinter den Geißen und neben dem Peter her, so leicht als nur eines aus der ganzen Gesellschaft. Der Peter hatte nicht Acht gegeben, was das Kind mache, als es zurückgeblieben war. Wie es nun in der neuen Bekleidung nachgesprungen kam, zog er lustig grinsend das ganze Gesicht auseinander und schaute zurück, und wie er unten das Häuflein Kleider liegen sah, ging sein Gesicht noch ein wenig mehr auseinander, und sein Mund kam fast von einem Ohr bis zum anderen; er sagte aber nichts. Wie nun das Kind sich so frei und leicht fühlte, fing es ein Gespräch mit dem Peter an, und er fing auch an zu reden und musste auf vielerlei antworten, denn das Kind wollte wissen, wie viele Geißen er habe und wohin er mit ihnen gehe und was er dort tue, wo er hinkomme. So langten endlich die Kinder samt den Geißen oben bei der Hütte an und kamen der Base Dete zu Gesicht. Kaum aber hatte diese die herankletternde Gesellschaft erblickt, als sie laut aufschrie: "Heidi, was machst du? Wie siehst du aus? Wo hast du deinen Rock und den zweiten und das Halstuch? Und ganz neue Schuhe habe ich dir gekauft auf den Berg und dir neue Strümpfe gemacht, und alles fort! Alles fort! Heidi, was machst du, wo hast du alles?"
gt_translation: Dete must have waited ten minutes and looked around to see if the children with the goats were nowhere to be seen; but when this was not the case, she climbed a little higher, where she could better see the whole pasture down, and from here she looked now here and there with signs of great impatience on her face and in her movements. Meanwhile the children were approaching by a long detour, for Peter knew many places where there were all kinds of good shrubs and bushes for his goats to gnaw on; therefore he made many turns on the way with his flock. At first the child had climbed in, panting in his heavy armor from the heat and discomfort and exhausting all his strength. He didn't say a word, but kept his eyes fixed on Peter, who jumped about effortlessly with his bare feet and light panties, and then on the goats, who with their thin, slender little legs climbed bushes and stones and steep slopes even more easily climbed up. Suddenly the child sat down on the floor, took off his shoes and stockings very quickly, stood up again, took off his thick red scarf, undid his skirt, took it off quickly and immediately had another one to crochet, because the Base Dete had put his Sunday dress over his everyday clothes, for the sake of brevity, so that nobody had to wear it. The everyday skirt was gone in a flash, and now the child was standing in a light petticoat, happily stretching his bare arms out of the short shirt sleeves into the air. Then she piled everything up nicely, and now she jumped and climbed after the goats and next to Peter, as easily as just one of the whole company. Peter hadn't paid any attention to what the child was doing when it stayed behind. As soon as she jumped in the new clothes, he spread his whole face, grinning merrily, and looked back, and when he saw the little pile of clothes lying below, his face spread a little more, and his mouth almost came up to one ear on the other hand; but he said nothing. As soon as the child felt so free and light, it started a conversation with Peter, and he also began to talk and had to answer many things, because the child wanted to know how many goats he had and where he was going with them and what he does where he goes. So at last the children, together with the goats, reached the hut upstairs and came face to face with Cousin Dete. But no sooner had she seen the company climbing up than she cried out loud: "Heidi, what are you doing? How do you look? Where are your skirts and the second one and the scarf? And I bought you brand new shoes on the mountain and I made you new stockings and everything's gone! Everything's gone! Heidi, what are you doing, where's everything?"

human_translations.translator_1: Deta waited about ten minutes to see if the children were coming up behind with the goats. As she could not find them anywhere, she climbed up a little higher to get a better view down the valley from there, and peered from side to side with marks of great impatience on her countenance. The children in the meantime were ascending slowly in a zigzag way, Peter always knowing where to find all sorts of good grazing places for his goats where they could nibble. Thus they strayed from side to side. The poor little girl had followed the boy only with the greatest effort and she was panting in her heavy clothes. She was so hot and uncomfortable that she only climbed by exerting all her strength. She did not say anything but looked enviously at Peter, who jumped about so easily in his light trousers and bare feet. She envied even more the goats that climbed over bushes, stones, and steep inclines with their slender legs. Suddenly sitting down on the ground the child swiftly took off her shoes and stockings. Getting up she undid the heavy shawl and the two little dresses. Out she slipped without more ado and stood up in only a light petticoat. In sheer delight at the relief, she threw up her dimpled arms, that were bare up to her short sleeves. To save the trouble of carrying them, her aunt had dressed her in her Sunday clothes over her workday garments. Heidi arranged her dresses neatly in a heap and joined Peter and the goats. She was now as light-footed as any of them. When Peter, who had not paid much attention, saw her suddenly in her light attire, he grinned. Looking back, he saw the little heap of dresses on the ground and then he grinned yet more, till his mouth seemed to reach from ear to ear; but he said never a word. The child, feeling free and comfortable, started to converse with Peter, and he had to answer many questions. She asked him how many goats he had, and where he led them, what he did with them when he got there, and so forth. When Deta saw the little party of climbers she cried out shrilly: "Heidi, what have you done? What a sight you are! Where are your dresses and your shawl? Are the new shoes gone that I just bought for you, and the new stockings that I made myself? Where are they all, Heidi?"
human_translations.translator_2: For several minutes after Barbie had left her, Detie looked anxiously about for the two children with the goats, but there was no sign of them. She climbed a little farther up the path to get a better view and then stopped to look again. She was getting very impatient. The children had strayed far away from the path, for Peter always went his own way up the mountain. What mattered was where his goats would find the best bushes and shrubs to nibble. At first Heidi had scrambled up after him, puffing and panting, for her load of clothes made climbing hard, hot work. She did not complain, but she looked enviously at Peter, running about so freely on bare feet, in comfortable trousers; and at the goats whose nimble little legs carried them so lightly up the steep slopes and over bushes and stones. Then suddenly she sat down and pulled off her boots and stockings. She unwound the thick red scarf and quickly unbuttoned her best dress, which Detie had made her wear on top of her everyday one, to save carrying it. She took off both dresses and stood there in nothing but a little petticoat, waving her bare arms in the air with delight. Then she laid all the clothes together in a neat pile and danced off to catch up with Peter and the goats. He had not noticed what she was doing, and when he caught sight of her running towards him like that, he smiled broadly. He looked back and saw the pile of clothing she had left on the grass, and grinned from ear to ear, but he said nothing. Heidi felt much happier, and free as air, and began to chatter away, asking him a string of questions. He had to tell her how many goats he had, where he was taking them, and what he was going to do when he got there. Presently they reached the hut and came within Detie’s view. As soon as she spotted them she called out shrilly: ‘What on earth have you been doing, Heidi? What a sight you look! What have you done with your frocks? And the scarf? And those good new boots I bought you to come up here in, and the stockings I knitted for you? Wherever have you left them all?’ Heidi calmly pointed to the place where she had undressed.
human_translations.translator_3: Meanwhile Heidi and the goatherd were climbing up by a far and roundabout way, for Peter knew many spots where all kinds of good food, in the shape of shrubs and plants, grew for his goats. The child, exhausted with the heat and weight of her thick clothes, panted and struggled after him, at first with some difficulty. She said nothing, but her little eyes kept watching first Peter, as he sprang nimbly hither and thither on his bare feet, clad only in his short, light breeches, and then the slim-legged goats that went leaping over rocks and shrubs. All at once she sat down on the ground, and began pulling off her shoes and stockings. Then she unwound the hot red shawl and took off her frock. But there was still another to unfasten, for Dete had put the Sunday dress on over the everyday one, to save the trouble of carrying it. Quick as lightning the everyday frock followed the other, and now the child stood up, clad only in her light short-sleeved under garment. She stretched out her little bare arms with glee. Leaving all her clothes together in a tidy little heap, she went jumping and climbing up after Peter and the goats as nimbly as any of the party. Now that Heidi was able to move at her ease, she began to enter into conversation with Peter. She asked him how many goats he had, where he was going to with them, and what he had to do when he arrived there. At last, after some time, they came within view of Dete. Hardly had the latter caught sight of the little company climbing up towards her when she shrieked out: "Heidi, what have you been doing! What a sight you have made of yourself! What can you have been thinking of, Heidi; where are all your clothes?"

Kaum aber hatte diese die herankletternde Gesellschaft erblickt, als sie laut aufschrie: "Heidi, was machst du? Wie siehst du aus? Wo hast du deinen Rock und den zweiten und das Halstuch? Und ganz neue Schuhe habe ich dir gekauft auf den Berg und dir neue Strümpfe gemacht, und alles fort! Alles fort! Heidi, was machst du, wo hast du alles?"
gt_translation: Dete must have waited ten minutes and looked around to see if the children with the goats were nowhere to be seen; but when this was not the case, she climbed a little higher, where she could better see the whole pasture down, and from here she looked now here and there with signs of great impatience on her face and in her movements. Meanwhile the children were approaching by a long detour, for Peter knew many places where there were all kinds of good shrubs and bushes for his goats to gnaw on; therefore he made many turns on the way with his flock. At first the child had climbed in, panting in his heavy armor from the heat and discomfort and exhausting all his strength. He didn't say a word, but kept his eyes fixed on Peter, who jumped about effortlessly with his bare feet and light panties, and then on the goats, who with their thin, slender little legs climbed bushes and stones and steep slopes even more easily climbed up. Suddenly the child sat down on the floor, took off his shoes and stockings very quickly, stood up again, took off his thick red scarf, undid his skirt, took it off quickly and immediately had another one to crochet, because the Base Dete had put his Sunday dress over his everyday clothes, for the sake of brevity, so that nobody had to wear it. The everyday skirt was gone in a flash, and now the child was standing in a light petticoat, happily stretching his bare arms out of the short shirt sleeves into the air. Then she piled everything up nicely, and now she jumped and climbed after the goats and next to Peter, as easily as just one of the whole company. Peter hadn't paid any attention to what the child was doing when it stayed behind. As soon as she jumped in the new clothes, he spread his whole face, grinning merrily, and looked back, and when he saw the little pile of clothes lying below, his face spread a little more, and his mouth almost came up to one ear on the other hand; but he said nothing. As soon as the child felt so free and light, it started a conversation with Peter, and he also began to talk and had to answer many things, because the child wanted to know how many goats he had and where he was going with them and what he does where he goes. So at last the children, together with the goats, reached the hut upstairs and came face to face with Cousin Dete. But no sooner had she seen the company climbing up than she cried out loud: "Heidi, what are you doing? How do you look? Where are your skirts and the second one and the scarf? And I bought you brand new shoes on the mountain and I made you new stockings and everything's gone! Everything's gone! Heidi, what are you doing, where's everything?"

human_translations.translator_1: Deta waited about ten minutes to see if the children were coming up behind with the goats. As she could not find them anywhere, she climbed up a little higher to get a better view down the valley from there, and peered from side to side with marks of great impatience on her countenance. The children in the meantime were ascending slowly in a zigzag way, Peter always knowing where to find all sorts of good grazing places for his goats where they could nibble. Thus they strayed from side to side. The poor little girl had followed the boy only with the greatest effort and she was panting in her heavy clothes. She was so hot and uncomfortable that she only climbed by exerting all her strength. She did not say anything but looked enviously at Peter, who jumped about so easily in his light trousers and bare feet. She envied even more the goats that climbed over bushes, stones, and steep inclines with their slender legs. Suddenly sitting down on the ground the child swiftly took off her shoes and stockings. Getting up she undid the heavy shawl and the two little dresses. Out she slipped without more ado and stood up in only a light petticoat. In sheer delight at the relief, she threw up her dimpled arms, that were bare up to her short sleeves. To save the trouble of carrying them, her aunt had dressed her in her Sunday clothes over her workday garments. Heidi arranged her dresses neatly in a heap and joined Peter and the goats. She was now as light-footed as any of them. When Peter, who had not paid much attention, saw her suddenly in her light attire, he grinned. Looking back, he saw the little heap of dresses on the ground and then he grinned yet more, till his mouth seemed to reach from ear to ear; but he said never a word. The child, feeling free and comfortable, started to converse with Peter, and he had to answer many questions. She asked him how many goats he had, and where he led them, what he did with them when he got there, and so forth. When Deta saw the little party of climbers she cried out shrilly: "Heidi, what have you done? What a sight you are! Where are your dresses and your shawl? Are the new shoes gone that I just bought for you, and the new stockings that I made myself? Where are they all, Heidi?"
human_translations.translator_2: For several minutes after Barbie had left her, Detie looked anxiously about for the two children with the goats, but there was no sign of them. She climbed a little farther up the path to get a better view and then stopped to look again. She was getting very impatient. The children had strayed far away from the path, for Peter always went his own way up the mountain. What mattered was where his goats would find the best bushes and shrubs to nibble. At first Heidi had scrambled up after him, puffing and panting, for her load of clothes made climbing hard, hot work. She did not complain, but she looked enviously at Peter, running about so freely on bare feet, in comfortable trousers; and at the goats whose nimble little legs carried them so lightly up the steep slopes and over bushes and stones. Then suddenly she sat down and pulled off her boots and stockings. She unwound the thick red scarf and quickly unbuttoned her best dress, which Detie had made her wear on top of her everyday one, to save carrying it. She took off both dresses and stood there in nothing but a little petticoat, waving her bare arms in the air with delight. Then she laid all the clothes together in a neat pile and danced off to catch up with Peter and the goats. He had not noticed what she was doing, and when he caught sight of her running towards him like that, he smiled broadly. He looked back and saw the pile of clothing she had left on the grass, and grinned from ear to ear, but he said nothing. Heidi felt much happier, and free as air, and began to chatter away, asking him a string of questions. He had to tell her how many goats he had, where he was taking them, and what he was going to do when he got there. Presently they reached the hut and came within Detie’s view. As soon as she spotted them she called out shrilly: ‘What on earth have you been doing, Heidi? What a sight you look! What have you done with your frocks? And the scarf? And those good new boots I bought you to come up here in, and the stockings I knitted for you? Wherever have you left them all?’ Heidi calmly pointed to the place where she had undressed.
human_translations.translator_3: Meanwhile Heidi and the goatherd were climbing up by a far and roundabout way, for Peter knew many spots where all kinds of good food, in the shape of shrubs and plants, grew for his goats. The child, exhausted with the heat and weight of her thick clothes, panted and struggled after him, at first with some difficulty. She said nothing, but her little eyes kept watching first Peter, as he sprang nimbly hither and thither on his bare feet, clad only in his short, light breeches, and then the slim-legged goats that went leaping over rocks and shrubs. All at once she sat down on the ground, and began pulling off her shoes and stockings. Then she unwound the hot red shawl and took off her frock. But there was still another to unfasten, for Dete had put the Sunday dress on over the everyday one, to save the trouble of carrying it. Quick as lightning the everyday frock followed the other, and now the child stood up, clad only in her light short-sleeved under garment. She stretched out her little bare arms with glee. Leaving all her clothes together in a tidy little heap, she went jumping and climbing up after Peter and the goats as nimbly as any of the party. Now that Heidi was able to move at her ease, she began to enter into conversation with Peter. She asked him how many goats he had, where he was going to with them, and what he had to do when he arrived there. At last, after some time, they came within view of Dete. Hardly had the latter caught sight of the little company climbing up towards her when she shrieked out: "Heidi, what have you been doing! What a sight you have made of yourself! And where are your two frocks and the red wrapper? And the new shoes I bought, and the new stockings I knitted for you—everything gone! not a thing left! What can you have been thinking of, Heidi; where are all your clothes?"
